entries.5fb795b9f6dbcb658887ae99ff898e37414facef: <div sID="gen22251" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="Matt.13" sID="Matt.13"/> <div eID="gen22251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22252" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22253" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, we have, I. The favour which Christ did to his countrymen in preaching the kingdom of heaven to them, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.1-Matt.13.2">ver. 1-2</reference>. He preached to them in parables, and here gives the reason why he chose that way of instructing, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.10-Matt.13.17">ver. 10-17</reference>. And the evangelist gives another reason, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.34-Matt.13.35">ver. 34, 35</reference>. There are eight parables recorded in this chapter, which are designed to represent the kingdom of heaven, the method of planting the gospel kingdom in the world, and of its growth and success. The great truths and laws of that kingdom are in other scriptures laid down plainly, and without parables: but some circumstances of its beginning and progress are here laid open in parables. 1. Here is one parable to show what are the great hindrances of people's profiting by the word of the gospel, and in how many it comes short of its end, through their own folly, and that is the parable of the four sorts of ground, delivered, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.3-Matt.13.9">ver. 3-9</reference>, and expounded, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.18-Matt.13.23">ver. 18-23</reference>. 2. Here are two parables intended to show that there would be a mixture of good and bad in the gospel church, which would continue till the great separation between them in the judgment day: the parable of the tares put forth (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.24-Matt.13.30">ver. 24-30</reference>), and expounded at the request of the disciples (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.36-Matt.13.43">ver. 36-43</reference>); and that of the net cast into the sea, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.47-Matt.13.50">ver. 47-50</reference>. 3. Here are two parables intended to show that the gospel church should be very small at first, but that in process of time it should become a considerable body: that of the grain of mustard-seed (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.31-Matt.13.32">ver. 31, 32</reference>), and that of the leaven, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.33">ver. 33</reference>. 4. Here are two parables intended to show that those who expect salvation by the gospel must be willing to venture all, and quit all, in the prospect of it, and that they shall be no losers by the bargain; that of the treasure hid in the field (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.44">ver. 44</reference>), and that of the pearl of great price, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.45-Matt.13.46">ver. 45, 46</reference>. 5. Here is one parable intended for direction to the disciples, to make use of the instructions he had given them for the benefit of others; and that is the parable of the good householder, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.51-Matt.13.52">ver. 51, 52</reference>. II. The contempt which his countrymen put upon him on account of the meanness of his parentage, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.53-Matt.13.58">ver. 53-58</reference>.
entries.198e65cd4a17a597057d2318bb3cd1d02270edb8: <div eID="gen22253" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22252" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Parable of the Sower; Why Christ Taught in Parables; Of the Sower and the Seed.</title> <div sID="gen22254" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The same day went Jesus out of the house, and sat by the sea side. <hi type="super">2</hi> And great multitudes were gathered together unto him, so that he went into a ship, and sat; and the whole multitude stood on the shore. <hi type="super">3</hi> And he spake many things unto them in parables, saying, Behold, a sower went forth to sow; <hi type="super">4</hi> And when he sowed, some <hi type="italic">seeds</hi> fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up: <hi type="super">5</hi> Some fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth: and forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth: <hi type="super">6</hi> And when the sun was up, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away. <hi type="super">7</hi> And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprung up, and choked them: <hi type="super">8</hi> But other fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit, some a hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold. <hi type="super">9</hi> Who hath ears to hear, let him hear. <hi type="super">10</hi> And the disciples came, and said unto him, Why speakest thou unto them in parables? <hi type="super">11</hi> He answered and said unto them, Because it is given unto you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it is not given. <hi type="super">12</hi> For whosoever hath, to him shall be given, and he shall have more abundance: but whosoever hath not, from him shall be taken away even that he hath. <hi type="super">13</hi> Therefore speak I to them in parables: because they seeing see not; and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand. <hi type="super">14</hi> And in them is fulfilled the prophecy of Esaias, which saith, By hearing ye shall hear, and shall not understand; and seeing ye shall see, and shall not perceive: <hi type="super">15</hi> For this people's heart is waxed gross, and <hi type="italic">their</hi> ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes they have closed; lest at any time they should see with <hi type="italic">their</hi> eyes, and hear with <hi type="italic">their</hi> ears, and should understand with <hi type="italic">their</hi> heart, and should be converted, and I should heal them. <hi type="super">16</hi> But blessed <hi type="italic">are</hi> your eyes, for they see: and your ears, for they hear. <hi type="super">17</hi> For verily I say unto you, That many prophets and righteous <hi type="italic">men</hi> have desired to see <hi type="italic">those things</hi> which ye see, and have not seen <hi type="italic">them;</hi> and to hear <hi type="italic">those things</hi> which ye hear, and have not heard <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">18</hi> Hear ye therefore the parable of the sower. <hi type="super">19</hi> When any one heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth <hi type="italic">it</hi> not, then cometh the wicked <hi type="italic">one,</hi> and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart. This is he which received seed by the way side. 20 But he that received the seed into stony places, the same is he that heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it; <hi type="super">21</hi> Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended. <hi type="super">22</hi> He also that received seed among the thorns is he that heareth the word; and the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word, and he becometh unfruitful. <hi type="super">23</hi> But he that received seed into the good ground is he that heareth the word, and understandeth <hi type="italic">it;</hi> which also beareth fruit, and bringeth forth, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. <div eID="gen22254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22255" type="x-p"/> We have here Christ preaching, and may observe, <div eID="gen22255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22256" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">When</hi> Christ preached this sermon; it was the same day that he preached the sermon in the foregoing chapter: so unwearied was he in doing good, and working the works of him that sent him. Note, Christ was for preaching both ends of the day, and has by his example recommended that practice to his church; we must <hi type="italic">in the morning sow our seed, and in the evening not withhold our hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.6">Eccl. xi. 6</reference>. An afternoon sermon well heard, will be so far from driving out the morning sermon, that it will rather clench it, and fasten the nail in a sure place. Though Christ had been in the morning opposed and cavilled at by his enemies, disturbed and interrupted by his friends, yet he went on with his work; and in the latter part of the day, we do not find that he met with such discouragements. Those who with courage and zeal break through difficulties in God's service, will perhaps find them not so apt to recur as they fear. Resist them, and they will flee. <div eID="gen22256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22257" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">To whom</hi> he preached; there were <hi type="italic">great multitudes gathered together to him,</hi> and they were the auditors; we do not find that any of the scribes or Pharisees were present. They were willing to hear him when he preached in the synagogue (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.9">ch. xii. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.14">14</reference>), but they thought it below them to hear a sermon by the sea-side, though Christ himself was the preacher: and truly he had better have their room than their company, for now they were absent, he went on quietly and without contradiction. Note, Sometimes there is most of the <hi type="italic">power</hi> of religion where there is least of the <hi type="italic">pomp</hi> of it: <hi type="italic">the poor receive the gospel.</hi> When Christ went to the <hi type="italic">sea-side, multitudes</hi> were presently <hi type="italic">gathered together to him.</hi> Where the king is, there is the court; where Christ is, there is the church, though it be by the sea-side. Note, Those who would get good by the word, must be willing to follow it in all its removes; when the ark shifts, shift after it. The Pharisees had been labouring, by base calumnies and suggestions, to drive the people off from following Christ, but they still flocked after him as much as ever. Note, Christ will be glorified in spite of all opposition; he will be followed. <div eID="gen22257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22258" type="x-p"/> 3. <hi type="italic">Where</hi> he preached this sermon. <div eID="gen22258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22259" type="x-p"/> (1.) His meeting-place was the sea-side. He went out of the house (because there was no room for the auditory) into the open air. It was pity but such a Preacher should have had the most spacious, sumptuous, and convenient place to preach in, that could be devised, like one of the Roman theatres; but he was now in his state of humiliation, and in this, as in other things, he denied himself the honours due to him; as he had not a house of his own to live in, so he had not a chapel of his own to preach in. By this he teaches us in the external circumstances of worship not to covet that which is stately, but to make the best of the conveniences which God in his providence allots to us. When Christ was born, he was crowded into the stable, and now to the sea-side, upon the strand, where all persons might come to him with freedom. He that was truth itself sought no corners (no <hi type="italic">adyta</hi>), as the pagan mysteries did. <hi type="italic">Wisdom crieth without,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.1.20">Prov. i. 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.13.20">John xiii. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen22259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22260" type="x-p"/> (2.) His pulpit was a ship; not like Ezra's pulpit, that was <hi type="italic">made for the purpose</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.8.4">Neh. viii. 4</reference>); but converted to this use for want of a better. No place amiss for such a Preacher, whose presence dignified and consecrated any place: let not those who preach Christ be ashamed, though they have mean and inconvenient places to preach in. Some observe, that the people stood upon dry ground and firm ground, while the Preacher was upon the water in more hazard. Ministers are most exposed to trouble. Here was a true rostrum, a ship pulpit. <div eID="gen22260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22261" type="x-p"/> 4. <hi type="italic">What</hi> and <hi type="italic">how</hi> he preached. (1.) <hi type="italic">He spake many things unto them.</hi> Many more it is likely than are here recorded, but all excellent and necessary things, things that belong to our peace, things pertaining to the kingdom of heaven: they were not trifles, but things of everlasting consequence, that Christ spoke of. It concerns us to give a more earnest heed, when Christ has so many things to say to us, that we miss not any of them. (2.) What he spake was in parables. A parable sometimes signifies any wise, weighty saying that is instructive; but here in the gospels it generally signifies a continued similitude or comparison, by which spiritual or heavenly things were described in language borrowed from the things of this life. It was a way of teaching used very much, not only by the Jewish rabbin, but by the Arabians, and the other wise men of the east; and it was found very profitable, and the more so from its being pleasant. Our Saviour used it much, and in it condescended to the capacities of people, and lisped to them in their own language. God had long <hi type="italic">used similitudes by his servants the prophets</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.10">Hos. xii. 10</reference>), and to little purpose; now he uses similitudes by his Son; surely they will reverence him who speaks from heaven, and of heavenly things, and yet clothes them with expressions borrowed from things earthly. See <reference osisRef="John.3.12">John iii. 12</reference>. So descending in a cloud. Now, <div eID="gen22261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22262" type="x-p"/> I. We have here the general reason why Christ taught in parables. The disciples were a little surprised at it, for hitherto, in his preaching, he had not much used them, and therefore they ask, <hi type="italic">Why speakest thou to them in parables?</hi> Because they were truly desirous that the people might hear with understanding. They do not say, Why speakest thou to <hi type="italic">us?</hi> (they knew how to get the parables explained) but to <hi type="italic">them.</hi> Note, We ought to be concerned for the edification of others, as well as for our own, by the word preached; and if ourselves be <hi type="italic">strong,</hi> yet to <hi type="italic">bear the infirmities of the weak.</hi> <div eID="gen22262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22263" type="x-p"/> To this question Christ answers largely, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.11-Matt.13.17">v. 11-17</reference>, where he tells them, that <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he preached by parables, because thereby the things of God were made more plain and easy to them who were willingly ignorant; and thus the gospel would be <hi type="italic">a savour of life</hi> to some, and <hi type="italic">of death</hi> to others. A parable, like the pillar of cloud and fire, turns a dark side towards Egyptians, which confounds them, but a light side towards Israelites, which comforts them, and so answers a double intention. The same light directs the eyes of some, but dazzles the eyes of others. Now, <div eID="gen22263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22264" type="x-p"/> 1. This reason is laid down (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Because it is given unto you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it is not given.</hi> That is, (1.) The disciples had knowledge, but the people had not. You know already something of these mysteries, and need not in this familiar way to be instructed; but the people are ignorant, are yet but babes, and must be taught as such by plain similitudes, being yet incapable of receiving instruction in any other way: for though they have eyes, they know not how to use them; so some. Or, (2.) The disciples were well inclined to the knowledge of gospel mysteries, and would search into the parables, and by them would be led into a more intimate acquaintance with those mysteries; but the carnal hearers that rested in bare hearing, and would not be at the pains to look further, nor to ask the meaning of the parables, would be never the wiser, and so would justly suffer for their remissions. A parable is a shell that keeps good fruit <hi type="italic">for</hi> the diligent, but keeps it <hi type="italic">from</hi> the slothful. Note, There are mysteries in the kingdom of heaven, and <hi type="italic">without controversy, great is the mystery of godliness:</hi> Christ's incarnation, satisfaction, intercession, our justification and sanctification by union with Christ, and indeed the whole work of redemption, from first to last, are <hi type="italic">mysteries,</hi> which could never have been discovered but by divine revelation (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.51">1 Cor. xv. 51</reference>), were at this time discovered but in part to the disciples, and will never be fully discovered till the veil shall be rent; but the mysteriousness of gospel truth should not discourage us from, but quicken us in, our enquiries after it and searches into it. [1.] It is graciously given to the disciples of Christ to be acquainted with these mysteries. Knowledge is the first gift of God, and it is a distinguishing gift (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.6">Prov. ii. 6</reference>); it was given to the apostles, because they were Christ's constant followers and attendants. Note, The nearer we draw to Christ, and the more we converse with him, the better acquainted we shall be with gospel mysteries. [2.] It is given to all true believers, who have an experimental knowledge of the gospel mysteries, and that is without doubt the best knowledge: a principle of grace in the heart, is that which makes men of quick understanding in <hi type="italic">the fear of the Lord,</hi> and in the faith of Christ, and so in the meaning of parables; and for want of that, Nicodemus, a master in Israel, talked of the <hi type="italic">new birth</hi> as a blind man of colours. [3.] There are those to <hi type="italic">whom this knowledge is not given,</hi> and a man can <hi type="italic">receive nothing unless it be given him from above</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.27">John iii. 27</reference>); and be it remembered that God is debtor to no man; his grace is his own; he gives or withholds it at pleasure (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.35">Rom. xi. 35</reference>); the difference must be resolved into God's sovereignty, as before, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.25-Matt.11.26">ch. xi. 25, 26</reference>. <div eID="gen22264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22265" type="x-p"/> 2. This reason is further illustrated by the rule God observes in dispensing his gifts; he bestows them on those who improve them, but takes them away from those who bury them. It is a rule among men, that they will rather entrust their money with those who have increased their estates by their industry, than with those who have diminished them by their slothfulness. <div eID="gen22265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22266" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here is a promise to him that has, that has true grace, pursuant to the election of grace, that has, and uses what he has; he shall have more abundance: God's favours are earnests of further favours; where he lays the foundation, he will build upon it. Christ's disciples used the knowledge they now had, and they had more abundance at the pouring out of the Spirit, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.1-Acts.2.13">Acts ii.</reference>. They who have the <hi type="italic">truth</hi> of grace, shall have the <hi type="italic">increase</hi> of grace, even to an abundance in glory, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Prov. iv. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">Joseph—he will add,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.30.24">Gen. xxx. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen22266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22267" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here is a threatening to him that has not, that has no desire of grace, that makes no right use of the gifts and graces he has: has not root, no solid principle; that has, but uses not what he has; from him shall be <hi type="italic">taken away</hi> that which he has or seems to have. His leaves shall wither, his gifts decay; the means of grace he has, and makes no use of, shall be taken from him; God will <hi type="italic">call in</hi> his talents out of their hands that are likely to become bankrupts quickly. <div eID="gen22267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22268" type="x-p"/> 3. This reason is particularly explained, with reference to the two sorts of people Christ had to do with. <div eID="gen22268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22269" type="x-p"/> (1.) Some were willingly ignorant; and such were amused by the parables (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.13">v. 13</reference>); <hi type="italic">because they seeing, see not.</hi> They had shut their eyes against the clear light of Christ's plainer preaching, and therefore were now left in the dark. Seeing Christ's person, they see not his glory, see no difference between him and another man; seeing his miracles, and hearing his preaching, they see not, they hear not with any concern or application; they understand neither. Note, [1.] There are many that see the gospel light, and hear the gospel sound, but it never reaches their hearts, nor has it any place in them. [2.] It is just with God to take away the light from those who shut their eyes against it; that such as will be ignorant, may be so; and God's dealing thus with them magnifies his distinguishing grace to his disciples. <div eID="gen22269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22270" type="x-p"/> Now in this the scripture would be fulfilled, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.14-Matt.13.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. It is quoted from <reference osisRef="Isa.6.9-Isa.6.10">Isa. vi. 9, 10</reference>. The evangelical prophet that spoke most plainly of gospel grace, foretold the contempt of it, and the consequences of that contempt. It is referred to no less than six times in the New Testament, which intimates, that in gospel times spiritual judgments would be most common, which make least noise, but are most dreadful. That which was spoken of the sinners in Isaiah's time was fulfilled in those in Christ's time, and it is still fulfilling every day; for while the wicked heart of man keeps up the same sin, the righteous hand of God inflicts the same punishment. Here is, <div eID="gen22270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22271" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First.</hi> A description of sinners' wilful blindness and hardness, which is their sin. <hi type="italic">This people's heart is waxed gross;</hi> it is <hi type="italic">fattened,</hi> so the word is; which denotes both sensuality and senselessness (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.70">Ps. cxix. 70</reference>); secure under the word and rod of God, and scornful as Jeshurun, that <hi type="italic">waxed fat and kicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.15">Deut. xxxii. 15</reference>. And when the heart is thus heavy, no wonder that the ears are dull of hearing; the whispers of the Spirit they hear not at all; the loud calls of the word, though the word be nigh them, they regard not, nor are at all affected by them: <hi type="italic">they stop their ears,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.58.4-Ps.58.5">Ps. lviii. 4, 5</reference>. And because they are resolved to be ignorant, they shut both the learning senses; for their eyes also they have closed, resolved that they would not see light come into the world, when the Son of Righteousness arose, but they shut their windows, because they <hi type="italic">loved darkness rather than light,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.19">John iii. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.5">2 Pet. iii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen22271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22272" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> A description of that judicial blindness, which is the just punishment of this. "<hi type="italic">By hearing, ye shall hear, and shall not understand;</hi> what means of grace you have, shall be to no purpose to you; though, in mercy to others, they are continued, yet in judgment to you, the blessing upon them is denied." The saddest condition a man can be in on this side hell, is to sit under the most lively ordinances with a dead, stupid, untouched heart. To hear God's word, and see his providences, and yet not to understand and perceive his will, either in the one or in the other, is the greatest sin and the greatest judgment that can be. Observe, It is God's work to <hi type="italic">give an understanding heart,</hi> and he often, in a way of righteous judgment, denies it to those to whom he has given the hearing ear, and the seeing eye, in vain. Thus does God choose sinners' delusions (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.4">Isa. lxvi. 4</reference>), and bind them over to the greatest ruin, by giving them up to their own hearts' lusts (<reference osisRef="Ps.81.11-Ps.81.12">Ps. lxxxi. 11, 12</reference>); <hi type="italic">let them alone</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.4.17">Hos. iv. 17</reference>); <hi type="italic">my Spirit shall not always strive,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.6.3">Gen. vi. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen22272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22273" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The woeful effect and consequence of this; <hi type="italic">Lest at any time they should see.</hi> They will not see because they will not turn; and God says that they shall not see, because they shall not turn: <hi type="italic">lest they should be converted, and I should heal them.</hi> <div eID="gen22273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22274" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. That seeing, hearing, and understanding, are necessary to conversion; for God, in working grace, deals with men as men, as rational agents; he draws with the cords of a man, changes the heart by opening the eyes, and turns <hi type="italic">from the power of Satan unto God,</hi> by turning first <hi type="italic">from darkness to light,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.18">Acts xxvi. 18</reference>). 2. All those who are truly converted to God, shall certainly be healed by him. "If they be converted I shall heal them, I shall save them:" so that if sinners perish, it is not to be imputed to God, but to themselves; they foolishly expected to be healed, without being converted. 3. It is just with God to deny his grace to those who have long and often refused the proposals of it, and resisted the power of it. Pharaoh, for a good while, hardened his own heart (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.15">Exod. viii. 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.32">32</reference>), and afterwards God hardened it, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.12">ch. ix. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.10.20">x. 20</reference>. Let us therefore fear, lest by sinning against the divine grace, we sin it away. <div eID="gen22274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22275" type="x-p"/> (2.) Others were effectually called to be the disciples of Christ, and were truly desirous to be taught of him; and they were instructed, and made to improve greatly in knowledge, by these parables, especially when they were expounded; and by them the things of God were made more plain and easy, more intelligible and familiar, and more apt to be remembered (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.16-Matt.13.17">v. 16, 17</reference>). <hi type="italic">Your eyes see, your ears hear.</hi> They saw the glory of God in Christ's person; they heard the mind of God in Christ's doctrine; they saw much, and were desirous to see more, and thereby were prepared to receive further instruction; they had opportunity for it, by being constant attendants on Christ, and they should have it from day to day, and grace with it. Now this Christ speaks of, <div eID="gen22275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22276" type="x-p"/> [1.] As a blessing; "<hi type="italic">Blessed are your eyes for they see, and your ears for they hear;</hi> it is your happiness, and it is a happiness for which you are indebted to the peculiar favour and blessing of God." It is a promised blessing, that in the days of the Messiah <hi type="italic">the eyes of them that see shall not be dim,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.3">Isa. xxxii. 3</reference>. The eyes of the meanest believer that knows experimentally the grace of Christ, are more blessed than those of the greatest scholars, the greatest masters in experimental philosophy, that are strangers to God; who, like the other gods they serve, <hi type="italic">have eyes, and see not. Blessed are your eyes.</hi> Note, True blessedness is entailed upon the right understanding and due improvement of the mysteries of the kingdom of God. The hearing ear and the seeing eye are God's work in those who are sanctified; they are the work of his grace (<reference osisRef="Prov.20.12">Prov. xx. 12</reference>), and they are a blessed work, which shall be fulfilled with power, when those who <hi type="italic">now see through a glass darkly, shall see face to face.</hi> It was to illustrate this blessedness that Christ said so much of the misery of those who are left in ignorance; <hi type="italic">they have eyes and see not;</hi> but <hi type="italic">blessed are your eyes.</hi> Note, The knowledge of Christ is a distinguishing favour to those who have it, and upon that account it lays under the greater obligations; see <reference osisRef="John.14.22">John xiv. 22</reference>. The apostles were to teach others, and therefore were themselves blessed with the clearest discoveries of divine truth. <hi type="italic">The watchmen shall see eye to eye,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.52.8">Isa. lii. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen22276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22277" type="x-p"/> [2.] As a transcendent blessing, desired by, but not granted to, many prophets and righteous men, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.17">v. 17</reference>. The Old-Testament saints, who had some glimpses, some glimmerings of gospel light, coveted earnestly further discoveries. They had the types, shadows, and prophecies, of those things but longed to see the Substance, that glorious end of those things which they could not steadfastly look unto; that glorious inside of those things which they could not look into. They desired to see the great Salvation, the Consolation of Israel, but did not see it, because the fulness of time was not yet come. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Those who know something of Christ, cannot but covet to know more. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The discoveries of divine grace are made, even to prophets and righteous men, but according to the dispensation they are under. Though they were the favourites of heaven, with whom God's secret was, yet they have not seen the things which they desired to see, because God had determined not to bring them to light yet; and his favours shall not anticipate his counsels. There was then, as there is still, a <hi type="italic">glory to be revealed;</hi> something in reserve, <hi type="italic">that they without us should not be made perfect,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.11.40">Heb. xi. 40</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> For the exciting of our thankfulness, and the quickening of our diligence, it is good for us to consider what means we enjoy, and what discoveries are made to us, now under the gospel, above what they had, and enjoyed, who lived under the Old-Testament dispensation, especially in the revelation of the atonement for sin; see what are the advantages of the New Testament above the Old (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.7 Heb.12.18">2 Cor. iii. 7, &c. Heb. xii. 18</reference>); and see that our improvements be proportionable to our advantages. <div eID="gen22277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22278" type="x-p"/> II. We have, in <reference osisRef="Matt.13.1-Matt.13.23">these verses</reference>, one of the parables which our Saviour put forth; it is that of the <hi type="italic">sower and the seed;</hi> both the parable itself, and the explanation of it. Christ's parables are borrowed from common, ordinary things, not from any philosophical notions or speculations, or the unusual phenomena of nature, though applicable enough to the matter in hand, but from the most obvious things, that are of every day's observation, and come within the reach of the meanest capacity; many of them are fetched from the husbandman's calling, as this of the sower, and that of the tares. Christ chose to do thus, 1. That spiritual things might hereby be made more plain, and, by familiar similitudes, might be made the more easy to slide into our understandings. 2. That common actions might hereby be spiritualized, and we might take occasion from those things which fall so often under our view, to meditate with delight on the things of God; and thus, when our hands are busiest about the world, we may not only notwithstanding that, but even with the help of that, be led to have our hearts in heaven. Thus the word of God shall talk with us, talk familiarly with us, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.22">Prov. vi. 22</reference>. <div eID="gen22278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22279" type="x-p"/> The parable of the sower is plain enough, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.3-Matt.13.9">v. 3-9</reference>. The exposition of it we have from Christ himself, who knew best what was his own meaning. The disciples, when they asked, <hi type="italic">Why speakest thou unto them in parables?</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.10">v. 10</reference>), intimated a desire to have the parable explained for the sake of the people; nor was it any disparagement to their own knowledge to desire it for themselves. Our Lord Jesus kindly took the hint, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the parable, directing his discourse to the disciples, but in the hearing of the multitude, for we have not the account of his dismissing them till <reference osisRef="Matt.13.36">v. 36</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Hear ye therefore the parable of the sower</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.18">v. 18</reference>); you have heard it, but let us go over it again." Note, It is of good use, and would contribute much to our understanding the word and profiting by it, to hear over again what we have heard (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.1">Phil. iii. 1</reference>); "You have heard it, but hear the interpretation of it." Note, <hi type="italic">Then</hi> only we hear the word aright, and to good purpose, when we understand what we hear; it is no hearing at all, if it be not with understanding, <reference osisRef="Neh.8.2">Neh. viii. 2</reference>. It is God's grace indeed that gives the understanding, but it is our duty to give our minds to understand. <div eID="gen22279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22280" type="x-p"/> Let us therefore compare the parable and the exposition. <div eID="gen22280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22281" type="x-p"/> (1.) The seed sown is the word of God, here called <hi type="italic">the word of the kingdom</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.19">v. 19</reference>): the kingdom of heaven, that is the kingdom; the kingdoms of the world, compared with that, are not to be called kingdoms. The gospel comes <hi type="italic">from</hi> that kingdom, and conducts <hi type="italic">to</hi> that kingdom; the word of the gospel is the word of the kingdom; it is the word of the King, and where that is, <hi type="italic">there is power;</hi> it is a law, by which we must be ruled and governed. This word is the seed sown, which seems a dead, dry thing, but all the product is virtually in it. It is <hi type="italic">incorruptible seed</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.23">1 Pet. i. 23</reference>); it is the gospel that <hi type="italic">brings forth fruit</hi> in souls, <reference osisRef="Col.1.5-Col.1.6">Col. i. 5, 6</reference>. <div eID="gen22281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22282" type="x-p"/> (2.) The sower that scatters the seed is our Lord Jesus Christ, either by himself, or by his ministers; see <reference osisRef="Matt.13.37">v. 37</reference>. The people are God's husbandry, his tillage, so the word is; and ministers are <hi type="italic">labourers together with God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.9">1 Cor. iii. 9</reference>. Preaching to a multitude is sowing the corn; we know not where it must light; only see that it be good, that it be clean, and be sure to give it seed enough. The sowing of the word is the sowing of a people for God's field, the <hi type="italic">corn of his floor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.21.10">Isa. xxi. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen22282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22283" type="x-p"/> (3.) The ground in which this seed is sown is the hearts of the children of men, which are differently qualified and disposed, and accordingly the success of the word is different. Note, Man's heart is like soil, capable of improvement, of bearing good fruit; it is pity it should lie fallow, or be like the field of the slothful, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.30">Prov. xxiv. 30</reference>. The soul is the proper place for the word of God to dwell, and work, and rule in; its operation is upon conscience, it is to light that candle of the Lord. Now according as we are, so the word is to us: <hi type="italic">Recipitur ad modum recipientis—The reception depends upon the receiver.</hi> As it is with the earth; some sort of ground, take ever so much pains with it, and throw ever so good seed into it, yet it brings forth no fruit to any purpose; while the good soil brings forth plentifully: so it is with the hearts of men, whose different characters are here represented by four sorts of ground, of which <hi type="italic">three</hi> are bad, and but <hi type="italic">one</hi> good. Note, The number of fruitless hearers is very great, even of those who heard Christ himself. <hi type="italic">Who has believed our report?</hi> It is a melancholy prospect which this parable gives us of the congregations of those who hear the gospel preached, that scarcely one in four brings forth fruit to perfection. Many are called with the common call, but in few is the eternal choice evidenced by the efficacy of that call, <reference osisRef="Matt.20.16">ch. xx. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen22283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22284" type="x-p"/> Now observe the characters of these four sorts of ground. <div eID="gen22284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22285" type="x-p"/> [1.] The highway ground, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.4-Matt.13.10">v. 4-10</reference>. They had pathways through their corn-fields (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.1">ch. xii. 1</reference>), and the seed that fell on them never entered, and so the birds picked it up. The place where Christ's hearers now stood represented the characters of most of them, the sand on the sea-shore, which was to the seed like the highway ground. <div eID="gen22285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22286" type="x-p"/> Observe <hi type="italic">First,</hi> What kind of hearers are compared to <hi type="italic">the highway ground;</hi> such as <hi type="italic">hear the word and understand it not;</hi> and it is their own fault that they do not. They take no heed to it, take no hold of it; they do not come with any design to get good, as the highway was never intended to be sown. They <hi type="italic">come before God as his people come, and sit before Him as his people sit;</hi> but it is merely for fashion-sake, to see and be seen; they mind not what is said, it comes in at one ear and goes out at the other, and makes no impression. <div eID="gen22286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22287" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> How they come to be unprofitable hearers. The <hi type="italic">wicked one,</hi> that is, the devil, <hi type="italic">cometh and catcheth away that which was sown.</hi>—Such mindless, careless, trifling hearers are an easy prey to Satan; who, as he is the great murderer of souls, so he is the great thief of sermons, and will be sure to rob us of the word, if we take not care to keep it: as the birds pick up the seed that falls on the ground that is neither ploughed before nor harrowed after. If we break not up the fallow ground, by preparing our hearts for the word, and humbling them to it, and engaging our own attention; and if we cover not the seed afterwards, by meditation and prayer; if we give not a <hi type="italic">more earnest heed to the things which we have heard,</hi> we are as the highway ground. Note, The devil is a sworn enemy to our profiting by the word of God; and none do more befriend his design than heedless hearers, who are thinking of something else, when they should be thinking of the things that belong to their peace. <div eID="gen22287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22288" type="x-p"/> [2.] The <hi type="italic">stony ground. Some fell upon stony places</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.5-Matt.13.6">v. 5, 6</reference>), which represents the case of hearers that go further than the former, who receive some good impressions of the word, but they are not lasting, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.20-Matt.13.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. Note, It is possible we may be a great deal better than some others, and yet not be so good as we should be; may go beyond our neighbours, and yet come short of heaven. Now observe, concerning these hearers that are represented by the stony ground, <div eID="gen22288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22289" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> How far they went. 1. They <hi type="italic">hear the word;</hi> they turn neither their backs upon it, nor a deaf ear to it. Note, hearing the word, though ever so frequently, ever so gravely, if we rest in that, will never bring us to heaven. 2. They are <hi type="italic">quick in hearing,</hi> swift to hear, <hi type="italic">he anon receiveth it,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">euthys</hi></hi>, he is ready to receive it, <hi type="italic">forthwith it sprung up</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.5">v. 5</reference>), it sooner appeared above ground than that which was sown in the good soil. Note, Hypocrites often get the start of true Christians in the shows of profession, and are often too hot to hold. He <hi type="italic">receiveth it straightway,</hi> without trying it; swallows it without chewing, and then there can never be a good digestion. Those are most likely to <hi type="italic">hold fast that which is good,</hi> that <hi type="italic">prove all things,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.21">1 Thess. v. 21</reference>. 3. They receive it with joy. Note, There are many that are very glad to hear a good sermon, that yet do not profit by it; they may be pleased with the word, and yet not changed and ruled by it; the heart may melt under the word, and yet not be melted down by the word, much less into it, as into a mould. Many <hi type="italic">taste the good word of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.5">Heb. vi. 5</reference>), and say they find sweetness in it, but some beloved lust is <hi type="italic">rolled under the tongue,</hi> which it would not agree with, and so they spit it out again. 4. They <hi type="italic">endure for awhile,</hi> like a violent motion, which continues as long as the impression of the force remains, but ceases when that has spent itself. Note, Many endure for awhile, that do not endure to the end, and so come short of the happiness which is promised to them only that persevere (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.22">ch. x. 22</reference>); they did run well, but something hindered them, <reference osisRef="Gal.5.7">Gal. v. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen22289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22290" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> How they fell away, so that no fruit was brought to perfection; no more than the corn, that having no depth of earth from which to draw moisture, is scorched and withered by the heat of the sun. And the reason is, <div eID="gen22290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22291" type="x-p"/> 1. They have <hi type="italic">no root in themselves,</hi> no settled, fixed principles in their judgments, no firm resolution in their wills, nor any rooted habits in their affections: nothing firm that will be either the sap or the strength of their profession. Note, (1.) It is possible there may be the green blade of a profession, where yet there is not the root of grace; hardness prevails in the heart, and what there is of soil and softness is only in the surface; inwardly they are no more affected than a stone; they have no root, they are not by faith united to Christ who is our Root; they derive not from him, they depend not on him. (2.) Where there is not a principle, though there be a profession, we cannot expect perseverance. Those who have no root will endure but awhile. A ship without ballast, though she may at first out-sail the laden vessel, yet will certainly fail in stress of weather, and never make her port. <div eID="gen22291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22292" type="x-p"/> 2. Times of trial come, and then they come to nothing. <hi type="italic">When tribulation and persecution arise because of the word, he is offended;</hi> it is a stumbling-block in his way which he cannot get over, and so he flies off, and this is all his profession comes to. Note, (1.) After a fair gale of opportunity usually follows a storm of persecution, to try who have received the word in sincerity, and who have not. When the word of Christ's kingdom comes to be the word of Christ's patience (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.10">Rev. iii. 10</reference>), then is the trial, who keeps it, and who does not, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.9">Rev. i. 9</reference>. It is wisdom to prepare for such a day. (2.) When trying times come, those who have no root are soon offended; they first quarrel with their profession, and then quit it; first find fault with it, and then throw it off. Hence we read of <hi type="italic">the offence of the cross,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.5.11">Gal. v. 11</reference>. Observe, Persecution is represented in the parable by <hi type="italic">the scorching sun,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.6">v. 6</reference>); the same sun which warms and cherishes that which was well rooted, withers and burns up that which wanted root. As the word of Christ, so the cross of Christ, is to some <hi type="italic">a savour of life unto life,</hi> to others <hi type="italic">a savour of death unto death:</hi> the same tribulation which drives some to apostasy and ruin, works for others <hi type="italic">a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory.</hi> Trials which shake some, confirm others, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.12">Phil. i. 12</reference>. Observe how soon they fall away, by and by; as soon rotten as they were ripe; a profession taken up without consideration is commonly let fall without it: "Lightly come, lightly go." <div eID="gen22292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22293" type="x-p"/> [3.] The thorny ground, <hi type="italic">Some fell among thorns</hi> (which are a good guard to the corn when they are in the hedge, but a bad inmate when they are in the field); <hi type="italic">and the thorns sprung up,</hi> which intimates that they did not appear, or but little, when the corn was sown, but afterwards they proved choking to it, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.7">v. 7</reference>. This went further than the former, for it had root; and it represents the condition of those who do not quite cast off their profession, and yet come short of any saving benefit by it; the good they gain by the word, being insensibly overcome and overborne by the things of the world. Prosperity destroys the word in the heart, as much as persecution does; and more dangerously, because more silently: the stones spoiled the root, the thorns spoil the fruit. <div eID="gen22293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22294" type="x-p"/> Now what are these choking thorns? <div eID="gen22294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22295" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First, The cares of this world.</hi> Care for another world would quicken the springing of this seed, but care for this world chokes it. Worldly cares are fitly compared to thorns, for they came in with sin, and are a fruit of the curse; they are good in their place to stop a gap, but a man must be well armed that deals much in them (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.6-2Sam.23.7">2 Sam. xxiii. 6, 7</reference>); they are entangling, vexing, scratching, and <hi type="italic">their end is to be burned,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.6.8">Heb. vi. 8</reference>. These thorns choke the good seed. Note, Worldly cares are great hindrances to our profiting by the word of God, and our proficiency in religion. They eat up that vigour of soul which should be spent in divine things; divert us from duty, distract us in duty, and do us most mischief of all afterwards; quenching the sparks of good affections, and bursting the cords of good resolutions; those who <hi type="italic">are careful and cumbered about many things,</hi> commonly neglect <hi type="italic">the one thing needful.</hi> <div eID="gen22295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22296" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The deceitfulness of riches. Those who, by their care and industry, have raised estates, and so the danger that arises from care seems to be over, and they <hi type="italic">continue hearers of the word,</hi> yet are still in a snare (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.4-Jer.5.5">Jer. v. 4, 5</reference>); it is <hi type="italic">hard for them to enter into the kingdom of heaven:</hi> they are apt to promise themselves that in riches which is not in them; to rely upon them, and to take an inordinate complacency in them; and this chokes the word as much as care did. Observe, It is not so much riches, as <hi type="italic">the deceitfulness of riches,</hi> that does the mischief: now they cannot be said to be deceitful to us unless we put our confidence in them, and raise our expectations from them, and then it is that they choke the good seed. <div eID="gen22296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22297" type="x-p"/> [4.] The good ground (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.18">v. 18</reference>); <hi type="italic">Others fell into good ground,</hi> and it is pity but that good seed should always meet with good soil, and then there is no loss; such are <hi type="italic">good hearers of the word,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.13.23">v. 23</reference>. Note, Though there are many that <hi type="italic">receive the grace of God,</hi> and the word of his grace, <hi type="italic">in vain,</hi> yet God has a remnant by whom it is received to good purpose; for God's <hi type="italic">word shall not return empty,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.55.10-Isa.55.11">Isa. lv. 10, 11</reference>. <div eID="gen22297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22298" type="x-p"/> Now that which distinguished this good ground from the rest, was, in one word, fruitfulness. By <hi type="italic">this</hi> true Christians are distinguished from hypocrites, that they <hi type="italic">bring forth the fruits of righteousness; so shall ye be my disciples,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.15.8">John xv. 8</reference>. He does not say that this good ground has no stones in it, or no thorns; but there were none that prevailed to hinder its fruitfulness. Saints, in this world, are not perfectly free from the remains of sin; but happily freed from the reign of it. <div eID="gen22298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22299" type="x-p"/> The hearers represented by the good ground are, <div eID="gen22299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22300" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Intelligent hearers; they <hi type="italic">hear the word and understand it;</hi> they understand not only the sense and meaning of the word, but their own concern in it; they understand it as a man of business understands his business. God in his word deals with men as men, in a rational way, and gains possession of the will and affections by opening the understanding: whereas Satan, who is <hi type="italic">a thief and a robber, comes not in by</hi> that <hi type="italic">door, but climbeth up another way.</hi> <div eID="gen22300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22301" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Fruitful hearers, which is an evidence of their good understanding: which <hi type="italic">also beareth fruit.</hi> Fruit is to every seed its own body, a substantial product in the heart and life, agreeable to the seed of the word received. We <hi type="italic">then</hi> bear fruit, when we practise according to the word; when the temper of our minds and the tenour of our lives are conformable to the gospel we have received, and we do as we are taught. <div eID="gen22301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22302" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Not all alike fruitful; <hi type="italic">some a hundred-fold, some sixty, some thirty.</hi> Note, Among fruitful Christians, some are more fruitful than others: where there is true grace, yet there are degrees of it; some are of greater attainments in knowledge and holiness than others; all Christ's scholars are not in the same form. We should aim at the highest degree, to bring <hi type="italic">forth a hundred-fold,</hi> as Isaac's ground did (<reference osisRef="Gen.26.12">Gen. xxvi. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">abounding in the work of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.15.8">John xv. 8</reference>. But if the ground be good, and the fruit right, the heart honest, and the life of a piece with it, those who bring forth but thirty-fold shall be graciously accepted of God, and it will be fruit abounding to their account, for <hi type="italic">we are under grace, and not under the law.</hi>
entries.0edaa5bd553b33d0f934e8f6777c2a4e582d84e9: <div eID="gen22302" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Parable of the Tares, the Mustard-Seed, the Leaven, &c..</title> <div sID="gen22303" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> Another parable put he forth unto them, saying, The kingdom of heaven is likened unto a man which sowed good seed in his field: <hi type="super">25</hi> But while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat, and went his way. <hi type="super">26</hi> But when the blade was sprung up, and brought forth fruit, then appeared the tares also. <hi type="super">27</hi> So the servants of the householder came and said unto him, Sir, didst not thou sow good seed in thy field? from whence then hath it tares? <hi type="super">28</hi> He said unto them, An enemy hath done this. The servants said unto him, Wilt thou then that we go and gather them up? <hi type="super">29</hi> But he said, Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them. <hi type="super">30</hi> Let both grow together until the harvest: and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn. <hi type="super">31</hi> Another parable put he forth unto them, saying, The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his field: <hi type="super">32</hi> Which indeed is the least of all seeds: but when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs, and becometh a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in the branches thereof. <hi type="super">33</hi> Another parable spake he unto them; The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened. <hi type="super">34</hi> All these things spake Jesus unto the multitude in parables; and without a parable spake he not unto them: <hi type="super">35</hi> That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying, I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things which have been kept secret from the foundation of the world. <hi type="super">36</hi> Then Jesus sent the multitude away, and went into the house: and his disciples came unto him, saying, Declare unto us the parable of the tares of the field. <hi type="super">37</hi> He answered and said unto them, He that soweth the good seed is the Son of man; <hi type="super">38</hi> The field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom; but the tares are the children of the wicked <hi type="italic">one;</hi> <hi type="super">39</hi> The enemy that sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels. <hi type="super">40</hi> As therefore the tares are gathered and burned in the fire; so shall it be in the end of this world. <hi type="super">41</hi> The Son of man shall send forth his angels, and they shall gather out of his kingdom all things that offend, and them which do iniquity; <hi type="super">42</hi> And shall cast them into a furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth. 43 Then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father. Who hath ears to hear, let him hear. <div eID="gen22303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22304" type="x-p"/> In these verses, we have, I. Another reason given why Christ preached by parables, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.34-Matt.13.35">v. 34, 35</reference>. <hi type="italic">All these things he spoke in parables,</hi> because the time was not yet come for the more clear and plain discoveries of the mysteries of the kingdom. Christ, to keep the people attending and expecting, preached in <hi type="italic">parables, and without a parable spake he not unto them;</hi> namely, at this time and in this sermon. Note, Christ tries all ways and methods to do good to the souls of men, and to make impressions upon them; if men will not be instructed and influenced by plain preaching, he will try them with parables; and the reason here given is, <hi type="italic">That the scripture might be fulfilled.</hi> The passage here quoted for it, is part of the preface to that historical Psalm, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.2">lxxviii. 2</reference>, <hi type="italic">I will open my mouth in a parable.</hi> What the Psalmist David, or Asaph, says there of his narrative, is accommodated to Christ's sermons; and that great precedent would serve to vindicate this way of preaching from the offence which some took at it. Here is, 1. The matter of Christ's preaching; he preached <hi type="italic">things which had been kept secret from the foundation of the world.</hi> The mystery of the gospel had been <hi type="italic">hid in God,</hi> in his councils and decrees, <hi type="italic">from the beginning of the world.</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.9">Eph. iii. 9</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Rom.16.25">Rom. xvi. 25</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7">1 Cor. ii. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.26">Col. i. 26</reference>. If we delight in the records of ancient things, and in the revelation of secret things, how welcome should the gospel be to us, which has in it such antiquity and such mystery! It was <hi type="italic">from the foundation of the world</hi> wrapt up in types and shadows, which are <hi type="italic">now done away;</hi> and those secret things are now become such things revealed <hi type="italic">as belong to us and to our children,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.29.29">Deut. xxix. 29</reference>. 2. The manner of Christ's preaching; he preached by parables; wise sayings, but figurative, and which help to engage attention and a diligent search. Solomon's sententious dictates, which are full of similitudes, are called <hi type="italic">proverbs,</hi> or <hi type="italic">parables;</hi> it is the same word; but in this, as in other things, <hi type="italic">Behold a greater than Solomon is here, in whom are hid treasures of wisdom.</hi> <div eID="gen22304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22305" type="x-p"/> II. The parable of the <hi type="italic">tares,</hi> and the exposition of it; they must be taken together, for the exposition explains the parable and the parable illustrates the exposition. <div eID="gen22305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22306" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. The disciples' request to their Master to have this parable expounded to them (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.36">v. 36</reference>); <hi type="italic">Jesus sent the multitude away;</hi> and it is to be feared many of them went away no wiser than they came; they had heard a sound of words, and that was all. It is sad to think how many go away from sermons without the word of grace in their hearts. Christ <hi type="italic">went into the house,</hi> not so much for his own repose, as for particular converse with his disciples, whose instruction he chiefly intended in all his preaching. He was ready to do good in all places; the disciples laid hold on the opportunity, and <hi type="italic">they came to him.</hi> Note, Those who would be wise for every thing else, must be wise to discern and improve their opportunities, especially of converse with Christ, of converse with him alone, in secret meditation and prayer. It is very good, when we return from the solemn assembly, to talk over what we have heard there, and by familiar discourse to help one another to understand and remember it, and to be affected with it; for we lose the benefit of many a sermon by vain and unprofitable discourse after it. See <reference osisRef="Luke.24.32">Luke xxiv. 32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.6.6-Deut.6.7">Deut. vi. 6, 7</reference>. It is especially good, if it may be, to ask of the ministers of the word the meaning of the word, for <hi type="italic">their lips should keep knowledge,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.2.7">Mal. ii. 7</reference>. Private conference would contribute much to our profiting by public preaching. Nathan's <hi type="italic">Thou art the man,</hi> was that which touched David to the heart. <div eID="gen22306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22307" type="x-p"/> The disciples' request to their Master was, <hi type="italic">Declare unto us the parable of the tares.</hi> This implied an acknowledgement of their ignorance, which they were not ashamed to make. It is probable they apprehended the general scope of the parable, but they desired to understand it more particularly, and to be assured that they took it right. Note, Those are rightly disposed for Christ's teaching, that are sensible of their ignorance, and sincerely desirous to be taught. He will <hi type="italic">teach the humble</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.8-Ps.25.9">Ps. xxv. 8, 9</reference>), but <hi type="italic">will for this be enquired of. If any man lack</hi> instruction, <hi type="italic">let him ask it of God.</hi> Christ had expounded the foregoing parable unasked, but for the exposition of this they ask him. Note, The mercies we have received must be improved, both for direction what to pray for, and for our encouragement in prayer. The first light and the first grace are given in a preventing way, further degrees of both which must be daily prayed for. <div eID="gen22307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22308" type="x-p"/> 2. The exposition Christ gave of the parable, in answer to their request; so ready is Christ to answer such desires of his disciples. Now the drift of the parable is, to represent to us the present and future state of the kingdom of heaven, the gospel church: Christ's care of it, the devil's enmity against it, the mixture that there is in it of good and bad in the other world. Note, The visible church is the kingdom of heaven; though there be many hypocrites in it, Christ rules in it as a King; and there is a remnant in it, that are the subjects and heirs of heaven, from whom, as the better part, it is denominated: the church is <hi type="italic">the kingdom of heaven</hi> upon earth. <div eID="gen22308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22309" type="x-p"/> Let us go over the particulars of the exposition of the parable. <div eID="gen22309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22310" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">He that sows the good seed is the Son of man.</hi> Jesus Christ is the Lord of the field, <hi type="italic">the Lord of the harvest,</hi> the Sower of good seed. When <hi type="italic">he ascended on high, he gave gifts to</hi> the world; not only good ministers, but other good men. Note, Whatever good seed there is in the world, it all comes from the hand of Christ, and is of his sowing: truths preached, graces planted, souls sanctified, are good seed, and all owing to Christ. Ministers are instruments in Christ's hand to sow good seed; are employed by him and under him, and the success of their labours depends purely upon his blessing; so that it may well be said, It is Christ, and no other, that sows the good seed; he <hi type="italic">is the Son of man,</hi> one of us, that his terror might not make us afraid; <hi type="italic">the Son of man,</hi> the Mediator, and that has authority. <div eID="gen22310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22311" type="x-p"/> (2.) <hi type="italic">The field is the world;</hi> the world of mankind, a large field, capable of bringing forth good fruit; the more is it to be lamented that it brings forth so much bad fruit: the world here is the visible church, scattered all the world over, not confined to one nation. Observe, In the parable it is called <hi type="italic">his field; the world</hi> is Christ's <hi type="italic">field,</hi> for <hi type="italic">all things are delivered unto him of the Father:</hi> whatever power and interest the devil has in the world, it is usurped and unjust; when Christ comes to take possession, he comes whose right it is; it is his field, and because it is his he took care to sow it with good seed. <div eID="gen22311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22312" type="x-p"/> (3.) <hi type="italic">The good seed are the children of the kingdom,</hi> true saints. They are, [1.] The <hi type="italic">children of the kingdom;</hi> not in profession only, as the Jews were (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.12">ch. viii. 12</reference>), but in sincerity; Jews inwardly, Israelites indeed, incorporated in faith and obedience to Jesus Christ the great King of the church. [2.] They are the good seed, precious as seed, <reference osisRef="Ps.126.6">Ps. cxxvi. 6</reference>. The seed is the substance of the field; so the holy seed, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.13">Isa. vi. 13</reference>. The seed is scattered, so are the saints; dispersed, here one and there another, though in some places thicker sown than in others. The seed is that from which fruit is expected; what fruit of honour and service God has from this world he has from the saints, whom he has <hi type="italic">sown unto himself in the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.2.23">Hos. ii. 23</reference>. <div eID="gen22312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22313" type="x-p"/> (4.) <hi type="italic">The tares are the children of the wicked one.</hi> Here is the character of sinners, hypocrites, and all profane and wicked people. [1.] They are the children of the devil, as a wicked one. Though they do not own his name, yet they bear his image, do his lusts, and from him they have their education; he rules over them, he works in them, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Eph. ii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.44">John viii. 44</reference>. [2.] They are tares in the field of this world; they do no good, they do hurt; unprofitable in themselves, and hurtful to <hi type="italic">the good seed,</hi> both by temptation and persecution: they are weeds in the garden, have the same rain, and sunshine, and soil, with the good plants, but are good for nothing: the <hi type="italic">tares are among the wheat.</hi> Note, God has so ordered it, that good and bad should be mixed together in this world, that the good may be exercised, the bad left inexcusable, and a difference made between earth and heaven. <div eID="gen22313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22314" type="x-p"/> (5.) <hi type="italic">The enemy that sowed the tares is the devil;</hi> a sworn enemy to Christ and all that is good, to the glory of the good God, and the comfort and happiness of all good men. He is an enemy to the field of the world, which he endeavours to make his own, by sowing his tares in it. Ever since he became a wicked spirit himself, he has been industrious to promote wickedness, and has made it his business, aiming therein to counterwork Christ. <div eID="gen22314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22315" type="x-p"/> Now concerning the sowing of the tares, observe in the parable, <div eID="gen22315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22316" type="x-p"/> [1.] That they were sown <hi type="italic">while men slept.</hi> Magistrates slept, who by their power, ministers slept, who by their preaching, should have prevented this mischief. Note, Satan watches all opportunities, and lays hold of all advantages, to propagate vice and profaneness. The prejudice he does to particular persons is when reason and conscience sleep, when they are off their guard; we have therefore need to <hi type="italic">be sober, and vigilant.</hi> It was in the night, for that is the sleeping time. Note, Satan rules in <hi type="italic">the darkness of this world;</hi> that gives him an opportunity to sow tares, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.20">Ps. civ. 20</reference>. It was <hi type="italic">while men slept;</hi> and there is no remedy but men must have some sleeping time. Note, It is as impossible for us to prevent hypocrites being in the church, as it is for the husbandman, when he is asleep, to hinder an enemy from spoiling his field. <div eID="gen22316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22317" type="x-p"/> [2.] The enemy, when he had sown the tares, <hi type="italic">went his way</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.25">v. 25</reference>), that it might not be known who did it. Note, When Satan is doing the greatest mischief, he studies most to conceal himself; for his design is in danger of being spoiled if he be seen in it; and therefore, when he comes to sow tares, he <hi type="italic">transforms himself into an angel of light,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.13-2Cor.11.14">2 Cor. xi. 13, 14</reference>. He <hi type="italic">went his way,</hi> as if he had done no harm; <hi type="italic">such is the way of the adulterous woman,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.30.20">Prov. xxx. 20</reference>. Observe, Such is the proneness of fallen man to sin, that if the enemy sow the tares, he may even go his way, they will spring up of themselves and do hurt; whereas, when good seed is sown, it must be tended, watered, and fenced, or it will come to nothing. <div eID="gen22317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22318" type="x-p"/> [3.] The tares appeared not till <hi type="italic">the blade sprung up, and brought forth fruit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.13.26">v. 26</reference>. There is a great deal of secret wickedness in the hearts of men, which is long hid under the cloak of a plausible profession, but breaks out at last. As the good seed, so the tares, lie a great while under the clods, and at first springing up, it is hard to distinguish them; but when a trying time comes, when fruit is to be brought forth, when good is to be done that has difficulty and hazard attending it, then you will return and discern between the sincere and the hypocrite: then you may say, This is wheat, and that is tares. <div eID="gen22318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22319" type="x-p"/> [4.] The servants, when they were aware of it, complained to their master (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.27">v. 27</reference>); <hi type="italic">Sir, didst thou not sow good seed in thy field?</hi> No doubt he did; whatever is amiss in the church, we are sure it is not of Christ: considering the seed which Christ sows, we may well ask, with wonder, <hi type="italic">Whence</hi> should <hi type="italic">these tares come?</hi> Note, The rise of errors, the breaking out of scandals, and the growth of profaneness, are matter of great grief to all the servants of Christ; especially to his faithful ministers, who are directed to complain of it to him whose the field is. It is sad to see such tares, such weeds, in the garden of the Lord; to see the good soil wasted, the good seed choked, and such a reflection cast on the name and honour of Christ, as if his field were no better than <hi type="italic">the field of the slothful, all grown over with thorns.</hi> <div eID="gen22319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22320" type="x-p"/> [5.] The Master was soon aware whence it was (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.28">v. 28</reference>); <hi type="italic">An enemy has done this.</hi> He does not lay the blame upon the servants; they could not help it, but had done what was in their power to prevent it. Note, The ministers of Christ, that are faithful and diligent, shall not be judged of Christ, and therefore should not be reproached by men, for the mixtures of bad with good, hypocrites with the sincere, in the field of the church. <hi type="italic">It must needs be that such offences will come;</hi> and they shall not be laid to our charge, if we do our duty, though it have not the desired success. Though they sleep, if they do not love sleep; though tares be sown, if they do not sow them nor water them, nor allow of them, the blame shall not lie at their door. <div eID="gen22320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22321" type="x-p"/> [6.] The servants were very forward to have these tares rooted up. "<hi type="italic">Wilt thou that we go</hi> and do it presently?" Note, The over-hasty and inconsiderate zeal of Christ's servants, before they have consulted with their Master, is sometimes ready, with the hazard of the church, to root out all that they presume to be tares: <hi type="italic">Lord, wilt thou that we call for fire from heaven?</hi> <div eID="gen22321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22322" type="x-p"/> [7.] The Master very wisely prevented this (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.29">v. 29</reference>); <hi type="italic">Nay, lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them.</hi> Note, It is not possible for any man infallibly to distinguish between tares and wheat, but he may be mistaken; and therefore such is the wisdom and grace of Christ, that he will rather permit the tares, than any way endanger the wheat. It is certain, scandalous offenders are to be censured, and we are to withdraw from them; those who are openly <hi type="italic">the children of the wicked one,</hi> are not to be admitted to special ordinances; yet it is possible there may be a discipline, either so mistaken in its rules, or so over-nice in the application of them, as may prove vexatious to many that are truly godly and conscientious. Great caution and moderation must be used in inflicting and continuing church censures, lest the wheat be trodden down, if not plucked up. The <hi type="italic">wisdom from above,</hi> as it <hi type="italic">is pure,</hi> so it is <hi type="italic">peaceable,</hi> and those who oppose themselves must not be cut off, but instructed, and <hi type="italic">with meekness,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.25">2 Tim. ii. 25</reference>. The tares, if continued under the means of grace, may become good corn; therefore have patience with them. <div eID="gen22322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22323" type="x-p"/> (6.) <hi type="italic">The harvest is the end of the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.13.39">v. 39</reference>. This world will have an end; though it continue long, it will not continue always; time will shortly be swallowed up in eternity. At the end of the world, there will be a great harvest-day, a day of judgment; at harvest all is ripe and ready to be cut down: both good and bad are ripe at the great-day, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.11">Rev. vi. 11</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">the harvest of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.15">Rev. xiv. 15</reference>. At harvest the reapers cut down all before them; not a field, not a corner, is left behind; so at the great day all must be judged (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.12-Rev.20.13">Rev. xx. 12, 13</reference>); God has <hi type="italic">set a harvest</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.11">Hos. vi. 11</reference>), and it shall not fail, <reference osisRef="Gen.8.22">Gen. viii. 22</reference>. At harvest every man reaps as he sowed; every man's ground, and seed, and skill, and industry, will be manifested: see <reference osisRef="Gal.6.7-Gal.6.8">Gal. vi. 7, 8</reference>. Then they who <hi type="italic">sowed precious seed, will come again with rejoicing</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.126.5-Ps.126.6">Ps. cxxvi. 5, 6</reference>), with <hi type="italic">the joy of harvest</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.3">Isa. ix. 3</reference>); when <hi type="italic">the sluggard, who would not plough by reason of cold, shall beg, and have nothing</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.20.4">Prov. xx. 4</reference>); shall cry, <hi type="italic">Lord, Lord,</hi> but in vain; when the harvest of those who sowed to the flesh, shall <hi type="italic">be a day of grief, and of desperate sorrow,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.17.11">Isa. xvii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen22323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22324" type="x-p"/> (7.) <hi type="italic">The reapers are the angels:</hi> they shall be employed, in the great day, in executing Christ's righteous sentences, both of approbation and condemnation, as ministers of his justice, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.31">ch. xxv. 31</reference>. The angels are skilful, strong, and swift, obedient servants to Christ, holy enemies to the wicked, and faithful friends to all the saints, and therefore fit to be thus employed. <hi type="italic">He that reapeth receiveth wages,</hi> and the angels will not be unpaid for their attendance; for <hi type="italic">he that soweth, and he that reapeth, shall rejoice together</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.4.36">John iv. 36</reference>); that <hi type="italic">is joy in heaven in the presence of the angels of God.</hi> <div eID="gen22324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22325" type="x-p"/> (8.) Hell-torments are the <hi type="italic">fire,</hi> into which the <hi type="italic">tares</hi> shall then be cast, and in which they shall be burned. At the great day a distinction will be made, and with it a vast difference; it will be a notable day indeed. <div eID="gen22325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22326" type="x-p"/> [1.] The tares will then be gathered out: <hi type="italic">The reapers</hi> (whose primary work it is to gather in the corn) shall be charged first to <hi type="italic">gather out the tares.</hi> Note, Though good and bad are together in this world undistinguished, yet at the great day they shall be parted; no tares shall then be among the wheat; no sinners among the saints: then you shall plainly discern <hi type="italic">between the righteous and the wicked,</hi> which here sometimes it is hard to do, <reference osisRef="Mal.3.18">Mal. iii. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mal.4.1">iv. 1</reference>. Christ will not bear always, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.1">Ps. l. 1</reference>, &c. They shall <hi type="italic">gather out of his kingdom all wicked things that offend, and all wicked persons that do iniquity: when he begins, he will make a full end.</hi> All those corrupt doctrines, worships, and practices, which have offended, have been scandals to the church, and stumbling-blocks to men's consciences, shall be condemned by the righteous Judge in that day, and consumed by <hi type="italic">the brightness of his coming;</hi> all <hi type="italic">the wood, hay, and stubble</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.12">1 Cor. iii. 12</reference>); and then <hi type="italic">woe to them that do iniquity, that make a trade of it,</hi> and persist in it; not only those in the last age of Christ's kingdom upon earth, but those in every age. Perhaps here is an allusion to <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.3">Zeph. i. 3</reference>, <hi type="italic">I will consume the stumbling-blocks with the wicked.</hi> <div eID="gen22326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22327" type="x-p"/> [2.] They will then be <hi type="italic">bound in bundles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.13.30">v. 30</reference>. Sinners of the same sort will be bundled together in the great day: a bundle of atheists, a bundle of epicures, a bundle of persecutors, and a great bundle of hypocrites.
