Those who have been associates in sin, will be so in shame and sorrow; and it will be an aggravation of their misery, as the society of glorified saints will add to their bliss. Let us pray, as David, <hi type="italic">Lord, gather not my soul with sinners</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.26.9">Ps. xxvi. 9</reference>), but let it be bound in <hi type="italic">the bundle of life, with the Lord our God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.29">1 Sam. xxv. 29</reference>. [3.] They will <hi type="italic">be cast into a furnace of fire;</hi> such will be the end of wicked, mischievous people, that are in the church as <hi type="italic">tares in the field;</hi> they are fit for nothing but fire; to it they shall go, it is the fittest place for them. Note, Hell is a furnace of fire, kindled by the wrath of God, and kept burning by the bundles of tares cast into it, who will be ever in the consuming, but never consumed. But he slides out of the metaphor into a description of those torments that are designed to be set forth by it: <hi type="italic">There shall be weeping, and gnashing of teeth;</hi> comfortless sorrow, and an incurable indignation at God, themselves, and one another, will be the endless torture of damned souls. Let us therefore, <hi type="italic">knowing these terrors of the Lord,</hi> be persuaded not to do iniquity. <div eID="gen22327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22328" type="x-p"/> (9.) Heaven is the <hi type="italic">barn</hi> into which all God's wheat shall be gathered in that harvest-day. <hi type="italic">But gather the wheat into my barn:</hi> so it is in the parable, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.30">v. 30</reference>. Note, [1.] In the field of this world good people are the wheat, the most precious grain, and the valuable part of the field. [2.] This wheat shall shortly be gathered, gathered from among the tares and weeds: all <hi type="italic">gathered together in a general assembly,</hi> all the Old-Testament saints, all the New-Testament saints, not one missing. <hi type="italic">Gather my saints together unto me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.5">Ps. l. 5</reference>. [3.] All God's wheat shall be lodged together in God's barn: particular souls are housed at death as a shock of corn (<reference osisRef="Job.5.26">Job v. 26</reference>), but the general in-gathering will be at the end of time: God's wheat will then be put together, and no longer scattered; there will be sheaves of corn, as well as bundles of tares: they will then be secured, and no longer exposed to wind and weather, sin and sorrow: no longer afar off, and at a great distance, in the field, but near, in the barn. Nay, heaven is a <hi type="italic">garner</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.12">ch. iii. 12</reference>), in which the wheat will not only be separated from the tares of ill companions, but sifted from the chaff of their own corruptions. <div eID="gen22328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22329" type="x-p"/> In the explanation of the parable, this is gloriously represented (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.43">v. 43</reference>); <hi type="italic">Then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father. First,</hi> It is their present honour, that God is their Father. <hi type="italic">Now are we the sons of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.3.2">1 John iii. 2</reference>); <hi type="italic">our Father in heaven</hi> is King there. Christ, when he went to heaven, went to his <hi type="italic">Father, and our Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.20.17">John xx. 17</reference>. It is our <hi type="italic">Father's house,</hi> nay, it is <hi type="italic">our Father's</hi> palace, his throne, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.21">Rev. iii. 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The honour in reserve for them is, that they <hi type="italic">shall shine forth as the sun in that kingdom.</hi> Here they are obscure and hidden (<reference osisRef="Col.3.3">Col. iii. 3</reference>), their beauty is eclipsed by their poverty, and the meanness of their outward condition; their own weaknesses and infirmities, and the reproach and disgrace cast upon them, cloud them; but then they shall shine forth as the sun from behind a dark cloud; at death they shall shine forth to themselves; at the great day they will shine forth publicly before all the world, <hi type="italic">their bodies will be made like Christ's glorious body:</hi> they shall shine by reflection, with a light borrowed from the Fountain of light; their sanctification will be perfected, and their justification published; God will own them for his children, and will produce the record of all their services and sufferings for his name: they shall shine as the sun, the most glorious of all visible beings. The glory of the saints is in the Old Testament compared to that of the firmament and the stars, but here to that of the sun; <hi type="italic">for life and immortality are brought to</hi> a much clearer <hi type="italic">light by the gospel,</hi> than under the law. Those who shine as lights in this world, that God may be glorified, shall shine as the sun in the other world, that <hi type="italic">they</hi> may be glorified. Our Saviour concludes, as before, with a demand of attention; <hi type="italic">Who hath ears to hear, let him hear.</hi> These are things which it is our happiness to hear of, and our duty to hearken to. <div eID="gen22329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22330" type="x-p"/> III. Here is the parable of the <hi type="italic">grain of mustard-seed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.13.31-Matt.13.32">v. 31, 32</reference>. The scope of this parable is to show, that the beginnings of the gospel <hi type="italic">would be small, but that its latter end would greatly increase.</hi> In this way the gospel church, <hi type="italic">the kingdom of God among us,</hi> would be <hi type="italic">set up in the world;</hi> in this way the work of grace in the heart, <hi type="italic">the kingdom of God within us,</hi> would be carried on in particular persons. <div eID="gen22330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22331" type="x-p"/> Now concerning the work of the gospel, observe, <div eID="gen22331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22332" type="x-p"/> 1. That it is commonly very weak and small at first, <hi type="italic">like a grain of mustard-seed, which is one of the least of all seeds.</hi> The kingdom of the Messiah, which was now in the setting up, made but a small figure; Christ and the apostles, compared with the grandees of the world, appeared <hi type="italic">like a grain of mustard-seed, the weak things of the world.</hi> In particular places, the first breaking out of the gospel light is but as <hi type="italic">the dawning of the day;</hi> and in particular souls, it is at first <hi type="italic">the day of small things,</hi> like a bruised reed. Young converts are like <hi type="italic">lambs</hi> that must be <hi type="italic">carried in his arms,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.40.11">Isa. xl. 11</reference>. There is a little faith, but there is much lacking in it (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.10">1 Thess. iii. 10</reference>), and the <hi type="italic">groanings</hi> such as <hi type="italic">cannot be uttered,</hi> they are so small; a principle of spiritual life, and some motion, but scarcely discernible. <div eID="gen22332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22333" type="x-p"/> 2. That yet it is growing and coming on. Christ's kingdom strangely got ground; great accessions were made to it; nations were born at once, in spite of all the oppositions it met with from hell and earth. In the soul where grace is true it will grow really, though perhaps insensibly. <hi type="italic">A grain of mustard-seed</hi> is small, but however it is seed, and has in it a disposition to grow. Grace will be getting ground, shining more and more, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Prov. iv. 18</reference>. Gracious habits confirmed, actings quickened, and knowledge more clear, faith more confirmed, love more inflamed; here is the seed growing. <div eID="gen22333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22334" type="x-p"/> 3. That it will at last come to a great degree of strength and usefulness; <hi type="italic">when it is grown to</hi> some maturity, <hi type="italic">it becomes a tree,</hi> much larger in those countries than in ours. The church, like <hi type="italic">the vine brought out of Egypt,</hi> has taken root, and <hi type="italic">filled the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.80.9-Ps.80.11">Ps. lxxx. 9-11</reference>. The church is like a great tree, in which the fowls of the air do lodge; God's people have recourse to it for food and rest, shade and shelter. In particular persons, the principle of grace, if true, will persevere and be perfected at last: growing grace will be strong grace, and will bring much to pass. Grown Christians must covet to be useful to others, as the mustard-seed when grown is to the birds; that those who dwell near or under their shadow may be the better for them, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.7">Hos. xiv. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen22334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22335" type="x-p"/> IV. Here is the parable of the <hi type="italic">leaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.13.33">v. 33</reference>. The scope of this is much the same with that of the foregoing parable, to show that the gospel should prevail and be successful by degrees, but silently and insensibly; the preaching of the gospel is like leaven, and works like leaven in the hearts of those who receive it. <div eID="gen22335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22336" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">A woman took</hi> this <hi type="italic">leaven;</hi> it was her work. Ministers are employed in leavening places, in leavening souls, with the gospel. <hi type="italic">The woman is the weaker vessel,</hi> and we have this treasure in such vessels. <div eID="gen22336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22337" type="x-p"/> 2. The leaven was <hi type="italic">hid in three measures of meal.</hi> The heart is, as the meal, soft and pliable; it is the tender heart that is likely to profit by the word: leaven among corn unground does not work, nor does the gospel in souls unhumbled and unbroken for sin: the law grinds the heart, and then the gospel leavens it. It is <hi type="italic">three measures of meal,</hi> a great quantity, for <hi type="italic">a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump.</hi> The meal must be kneaded, before it receive the leaven; our hearts, as they must be broken, so they must be moistened, and pains taken with them to prepare them for the word, that they may receive the impressions of it. The leaven must be <hi type="italic">hid in the heart</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.11">Ps. cxix. 11</reference>), not so much for secrecy (for it will show itself) as for safety; our inward thought must be upon it, we must lay it up, as Mary laid up the sayings of Christ, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.51">Luke ii. 51</reference>. When the woman hides the leaven in the meal, it is with an intention that it should communicate its taste and relish to it; so we must treasure up the word in our souls, that we may be sanctified by it, <reference osisRef="John.17.17">John xvii. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen22337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22338" type="x-p"/> 3. The leaven thus hid in the dough, works there, it ferments; <hi type="italic">the word is quick and powerful,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.4.12">Heb. iv. 12</reference>. The leaven works speedily, so does the word, and yet gradually. What a sudden change did Elijah's mantle make upon Elisha! <reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.20">1 Kings xix. 20</reference>. It works silently and insensibly (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.26">Mark iv. 26</reference>), yet strongly and irresistibly: it does its work without noise, for so is <hi type="italic">the way of the Spirit,</hi> but does it without fail. Hide but the leaven in the dough, and all the world cannot hinder it from communicating its taste and relish to it, and yet none sees how it is done, but by degrees <hi type="italic">the whole is leavened.</hi> <div eID="gen22338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22339" type="x-p"/> (1.) Thus it was in the world. The apostles, by their preaching, hid a handful of leaven in the great mass of mankind, and it had a strange effect; it put the world into a ferment, and in a sense turned it <hi type="italic">upside down</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.6">Acts xvii. 6</reference>), and by degrees made a wonderful change in the taste and relish of it: the savour of the gospel was <hi type="italic">manifested in every place,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.14">2 Cor. ii. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.15.19">Rom. xv. 19</reference>. It was thus effectual, not by outward force, and therefore not by any such force resistible and conquerable, but by <hi type="italic">the Spirit of the Lord of hosts, who works, and none can hinder.</hi> <div eID="gen22339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22340" type="x-p"/> (2.) Thus it is in the heart. When the gospel comes into the soul, [1.] It works a change, not in the substance; the dough is the same, but in the quality; it makes us to savour otherwise than we have done, and other things to savour with us otherwise than they used to do, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.5">Rom. viii. 5</reference>. [2.] It works a universal change; it diffuses itself into all the powers and faculties of the soul, and alters the property even of the members of the body, <reference osisRef="Rom.6.13">Rom. vi. 13</reference>. [3.] This change is such as makes the soul to partake of the nature of the word, as the dough does of the leaven. We are delivered into it as into a mould (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.17">Rom. vi. 17</reference>), changed into the same image (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2 Cor. iii. 18</reference>), like the impression of the seal upon the wax. The gospel savours of God, and Christ, and free grace, and another world, and these things now relish with the soul. It is a word of faith and repentance, holiness and love, and these are wrought in the soul by it. This savour is communicated insensibly, for <hi type="italic">our life is hid;</hi> but inseparably, for grace is a <hi type="italic">good part that shall never be taken away</hi> from those who have it. When the dough is leavened, then to the oven with it; trials and afflictions commonly attend this change; but thus saints are fitted to be bread for our Master's table.
entries.054e6d4af9008365c60bfa85d8f4bde1956a2aba: <div eID="gen22340" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Various Parables.</title> <div sID="gen22341" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">44</hi> Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field. <hi type="super">45</hi> Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls: <hi type="super">46</hi> Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it. <hi type="super">47</hi> Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a net, that was cast into the sea, and gathered of every kind: 48 Which, when it was full, they drew to shore, and sat down, and gathered the good into vessels, but cast the bad away. 49 So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just, <hi type="super">50</hi> And shall cast them into the furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth. <hi type="super">51</hi> Jesus saith unto them, Have ye understood all these things? They say unto him, Yea, Lord. <hi type="super">52</hi> Then said he unto them, Therefore every scribe <hi type="italic">which is</hi> instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man <hi type="italic">that is</hi> a householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure <hi type="italic">things</hi> new and old. <div eID="gen22341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22342" type="x-p"/> We have four short parables in these verses. <div eID="gen22342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22343" type="x-p"/> I. That of the <hi type="italic">treasure hid in the field.</hi> Hitherto he had compared <hi type="italic">the kingdom of heaven</hi> to small things, because its beginning was small; but, lest any should thence take occasion to think meanly of it, in this parable and the next he represents it as of great value in itself, and of great advantage to those who embrace it, and are willing to come up to its terms; it is here likened <hi type="italic">to a treasure hid in the field,</hi> which, if we will, we may make our own. <div eID="gen22343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22344" type="x-p"/> 1. Jesus Christ is the true Treasure; in him there is an abundance of all that which is rich and useful, and will be a portion for us: <hi type="italic">all fulness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.1.19">Col. i. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.16">John i. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">treasures of wisdom and knowledge</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.2.3">Col. ii. 3</reference>), of righteousness, grace, and peace; these are laid up for us in Christ; and, if we have an interest in him, it is all our own. <div eID="gen22344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22345" type="x-p"/> 2. The gospel is the field in which this treasure is hid: it is hid in the word of the gospel, both the Old-Testament and the New-Testament gospel. In gospel ordinances it is hid as the milk in the breast, the marrow in the bone, the manna in the dew, the water in the well (<reference osisRef="Isa.12.3">Isa. xii. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">the honey in the honey-comb.</hi> It is hid, not <hi type="italic">in a garden enclosed,</hi> or <hi type="italic">a spring shut up,</hi> but <hi type="italic">in a field,</hi> an open field; <hi type="italic">whoever will, let him come, and search the scriptures;</hi> let him dig in <hi type="italic">this field</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.4">Prov. ii. 4</reference>); and whatever royal mines we find, they are all our own, if we take the right course. <div eID="gen22345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22346" type="x-p"/> 3. It is a great thing to discover the treasure hid in this field, and the unspeakable value of it. The reason why so many slight the gospel, and will not be at the expense, and run the hazard, of entertaining it, is because they look only upon the surface of the field, and judge by that, and so see no excellency in the Christian institutes above those of the philosophers; nay, the richest mines are often in grounds that appear most barren; and therefore they will not so much as bid for the field, much less come up to the price. <hi type="italic">What is thy beloved more than another beloved?</hi> What is the Bible more than other good books? The gospel of Christ more than Plato's philosophy, or Confucius's morals: but those who have <hi type="italic">searched the scriptures,</hi> so as in them to find Christ and <hi type="italic">eternal life</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.39">John v. 39</reference>), have discovered such a treasure in this field as makes it infinitely more valuable. <div eID="gen22346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22347" type="x-p"/> 4. Those who discern this treasure in the field, and value it aright, will never be easy till they have made it their own upon any terms. He that has found this treasure, hides it, which denotes a holy jealousy, <hi type="italic">lest we come short</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.4.1">Heb. iv. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">looking diligently</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.15">Heb. xii. 15</reference>), lest Satan come between us and it. He rejoices in it, though as yet the bargain be not made; he is glad there is such a bargain to be had, and that he is in a fair way to have an interest in Christ; that the matter is in treaty: their <hi type="italic">hearts</hi> may <hi type="italic">rejoice,</hi> who are yet <hi type="italic">but seeking the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.105.3">Ps. cv. 3</reference>. He resolves to <hi type="italic">buy this field:</hi> they who embrace gospel offers, upon gospel terms, buy this field; they make it their own, for the sake of the unseen treasure in it. It is Christ in the gospel that we are to have an eye to; we need not go up to heaven, but Christ in the word is nigh us. And so intent he is upon it, <hi type="italic">that he sells all to buy this field:</hi> they who would have saving benefit by Christ, must be willing to part with all, that they may make it sure to themselves; must <hi type="italic">count every thing but loss, that they may win Christ, and be found in him.</hi> <div eID="gen22347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22348" type="x-p"/> II. That of <hi type="italic">the pearl of price</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.45-Matt.13.46">v. 45, 46</reference>), which is to the same purport with the former, of the treasure. <hi type="italic">The dream is thus doubled, for the thing is certain.</hi> <div eID="gen22348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22349" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. All the children of men are busy, <hi type="italic">seeking goodly pearls:</hi> one would be rich, another would be honourable, another would be learned; but the most are imposed upon, and take up with counterfeits for pearls. <div eID="gen22349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22350" type="x-p"/> 2. Jesus Christ is a <hi type="italic">Pearl of great price,</hi> a Jewel of inestimable value, which will make those who have it rich, truly rich, rich toward God; in having him, we have enough to make us happy here and for ever. <div eID="gen22350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22351" type="x-p"/> 3. A true Christian is a spiritual <hi type="italic">merchant,</hi> that seeks and finds this pearl of price; that does not take up with any thing short of an interest in Christ, and, as one that is resolved to be spiritually rich, trades high: <hi type="italic">He went and bought that pearl;</hi> did not only bid for it, but purchased it. What will it avail us to know Christ, if we do not know him as ours, <hi type="italic">made to us wisdom?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">1 Cor. i. 30</reference>. <div eID="gen22351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22352" type="x-p"/> 4. Those who would have a saving interest in Christ, must be willing to part with all for him, leave all to follow him. Whatever stands in opposition to Christ, or in competition with him for our love and service, we must cheerfully quit it, though ever so dear to us. A man may buy gold too dear, but not this pearl of price. <div eID="gen22352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22353" type="x-p"/> III. That of the <hi type="italic">net cast into the sea,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.13.47-Matt.13.49">v. 47-49</reference>. <div eID="gen22353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22354" type="x-p"/> 1. Here is the parable itself. Where note, (1.) The world is a vast sea, and the children of men <hi type="italic">are things creeping innumerable, both small and great,</hi> in that sea, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.25">Ps. civ. 25</reference>. Men in their natural state are <hi type="italic">like the fishes of the sea</hi> that have no ruler over them, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.14">Hab. i. 14</reference>. (2.) The preaching of the gospel is the casting of a net into this sea, to catch something out of it, for his glory who has the sovereignty of the sea. Ministers are <hi type="italic">fishers of men,</hi> employed in casting and drawing this net; and <hi type="italic">then</hi> they speed, when at Christ's word they let down the net; otherwise, they <hi type="italic">toil and catch nothing.</hi> (3.) This net gathers of every kind, as large dragnets do. In the visible church there is a deal of trash and rubbish, dirt and weeds and vermin, as well as fish. (4.) There is a time coming when this net will be full, and drawn to the shore; a set time when the gospel shall have fulfilled that for which it was sent, and we are sure it shall not return void, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.10-Isa.55.11">Isa. lv. 10, 11</reference>. The net is now filling; sometimes it fills faster than at other times, but still it fills, and will be drawn to shore, when the <hi type="italic">mystery of God shall be finished.</hi> (5.) When the net is full and drawn to the shore, there shall be a separation between the good and bad that were gathered in it. Hypocrites and true Christians shall then be parted; the good shall be gathered into vessels, as valuable, and therefore to be carefully kept, but the bad shall be cast away, as vile and unprofitable; and miserable is the condition of those who are cast away in that day. While the net is in the sea, it is not known what is in it, the fishermen themselves cannot distinguish; but they carefully draw it, and all that is in it, to the shore, for the sake of the good that is in it. Such is God's care for the visible church, and such should ministers' concern be for those under their charge, though they are mixed. <div eID="gen22354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22355" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is the explanation of the latter part of the parable, the former is obvious and plain enough: we see gathered in the visible church, <hi type="italic">some of every kind:</hi> but the latter part refers to that which is yet to come, and is therefore more particularly explained, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.49-Matt.13.50">v. 49, 50</reference>. <hi type="italic">So shall it be at the end of the world;</hi> then, and not till then, will the dividing, discovering day be. We must not look for the net full of all good fish; the vessels will be so, but in the net they are mixed. See here, (1.) The distinguishing of the wicked from the righteous. The angels of heaven shall come forth to do that which the angels of the churches could never do; they shall <hi type="italic">sever the wicked from among the just;</hi> and we need not ask how they will distinguish them when they have both their commission and their instructions from him that knows all men, and particularly knows them that are <hi type="italic">his,</hi> and them that are <hi type="italic">not,</hi> and we may be sure there shall be no mistake or blunder either way. (2.) The doom of the wicked when they are thus severed. They shall be <hi type="italic">cast into the furnace,</hi> Note, Everlasting misery and sorrow will certainly be the portion of those who live among sanctified ones, but themselves die unsanctified. This is the same with what we had before, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.42">v. 42</reference>. Note, Christ himself preached often of hell-torments, as the everlasting punishment of hypocrites; and it is good for us to be often reminded of this awakening, quickening truth. <div eID="gen22355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22356" type="x-p"/> IV. Here is the parable of the <hi type="italic">good householder,</hi> which is intended to rivet all the rest. <div eID="gen22356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22357" type="x-p"/> 1. The occasion of it was the good proficiency which the disciples had made in learning, and their profiting by this sermon in particular. (1.) He asked them, <hi type="italic">Have ye understood all these things?</hi> Intimating, that if they had not, he was ready to explain what they did not understand. Note, It is the will of Christ, that all those who read and hear the word should understand it; for otherwise how should they get good by it? It is therefore good for us, when we have read or heard the word, to examine ourselves, or to be examined, whether we have understood it or not. It is no disparagement to the disciples of Christ to be catechised. Christ invites us to seek to him for instruction, and ministers should proffer their service to those who have any good question to ask concerning what they have heard. (2.) They answered him, <hi type="italic">Yea, Lord:</hi> and we have reason to believe they said true, because, when they did not understand, they asked for an explication, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.36">v. 36</reference>. And the exposition of that parable was a key to the rest. Note, The right understanding of one good sermon, will very much help us to understand another; for good truths mutually explain and illustrate one another; and <hi type="italic">knowledge is easy to him that understandeth.</hi> <div eID="gen22357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22358" type="x-p"/> 2. The scope of the parable itself was to give his approbation and commendation of their proficiency. Note, Christ is ready to encourage willing learners in his school, though they are but weak; and to say, <hi type="italic">Well done, well said.</hi> <div eID="gen22358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22359" type="x-p"/> (1.) He commends them as <hi type="italic">scribes instructed unto the kingdom of heaven.</hi> They were now learning that they might teach, and the teachers among the Jews were the scribes. Ezra, who <hi type="italic">prepared his heart to teach in Israel,</hi> is called <hi type="italic">a ready scribe,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.6">Ezra vii. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.10">10</reference>. Now a skilful, faithful minister of the gospel is a scribe too; but for distinction, he is called a scribe <hi type="italic">instructed unto the kingdom of heaven,</hi> well versed in the things of the gospel, and well able to teach those things. Note, [1.] Those who are to instruct others, have need to be well instructed themselves. If the priest's lips must keep knowledge, his head must first have knowledge. [2.] The instruction of a gospel minister must be in the <hi type="italic">kingdom of heaven,</hi> that is it about which his business lies. A man may be a great philosopher and politician, and yet if not instructed to the kingdom of heaven, he will make but a bad minister. <div eID="gen22359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22360" type="x-p"/> (2.) He compares them to a good householder, who <hi type="italic">brings forth out of his treasure things new and old;</hi> fruits of last year's growth and this year's gathering, abundance and variety, for the entertainment of his friends, <reference osisRef="Song.7.13">Cant. vii. 13</reference>. See here, [1.] What should be a minister's furniture, <hi type="italic">a treasure of things new and old.</hi> Those who have so many and various occasions, have need to stock themselves well in their gathering days with truths new and old, out of the Old Testament and out of the new; with ancient and modern improvements, <hi type="italic">that the man of God may be thoroughly furnished,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.16-2Tim.3.17">2 Tim. iii. 16, 17</reference>. Old experiences, and new observations, all have their use; and we must not content ourselves with old discoveries, but must be adding new. Live and learn. [2.] What use he should make of this furniture; he should <hi type="italic">bring forth:</hi> laying up is in order to laying out, for the benefit of others. <hi type="italic">Sic vox non vobis—You are to lay up, but not for yourselves.</hi> Many are full, but they have no vent (<reference osisRef="Job.32.19">Job xxxii. 19</reference>); have a talent, but they bury it; such are unprofitable servants; Christ himself received that he might give; so must we, and we shall have more. In bringing forth, things new and old do best together; old truths, but new methods and expressions, especially new affections.
entries.1ca4ba8a4e631f3a7057e5d1f8488fc46059a0f8: <div eID="gen22360" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Contempt of Christ by His Countrymen.</title> <div sID="gen22361" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">53</hi> And it came to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> when Jesus had finished these parables, he departed thence. <hi type="super">54</hi> And when he was come into his own country, he taught them in their synagogue, insomuch that they were astonished, and said, Whence hath this <hi type="italic">man</hi> this wisdom, and <hi type="italic">these</hi> mighty works? 55 Is not this the carpenter's son? is not his mother called Mary? and his brethren, James, and Joses, and Simon, and Judas? 56 And his sisters, are they not all with us? Whence then hath this <hi type="italic">man</hi> all these things? <hi type="super">57</hi> And they were offended in him. But Jesus said unto them, A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country, and in his own house. <hi type="super">58</hi> And he did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief. <div eID="gen22361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22362" type="x-p"/> We have here Christ in his own country. He went about doing good, yet left not any place till he had finished his testimony there at that time. His own countrymen had rejected him once, yet he came to them again. Note, Christ does not take refusers at their first word, but repeats his offers to those who have often repulsed them. In this, as in other things, Christ was like his brethren; he had a natural affection to his own country; <hi type="italic">Patriam quisque amat, non quia pulchram, sed quia suam—Every one loves his country, not because it is beautiful, but because it is his own.</hi> Seneca. His treatment this time was much the same as before, scornful and spiteful. Observe, <div eID="gen22362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22363" type="x-p"/> I. How they expressed their contempt of him. When he <hi type="italic">taught them in their synagogue, they were astonished;</hi> not that they were taken with his preaching, or admired his doctrine in itself, but only that it should be his; looking upon him as unlikely to be such a teacher. Two things they upbraided him with. <div eID="gen22363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22364" type="x-p"/> 1. His want of academical education. They owned that he had wisdom, and did mighty works; but the question was, Whence he had them: for they knew that he was not brought up at the feet of the rabbin: he had never been at the university, nor taken his degree, nor was called of men, <hi type="italic">Rabbi, Rabbi.</hi> Note, Mean and prejudiced spirits are apt to judge of men by their education, and to enquire more into their rise than into their reasons. "<hi type="italic">Whence has this man these mighty works?</hi> Did he come honestly by them? Has he not been studying the black art?" Thus they turned that against him which was really for him; for if they had not been wilfully blind, they must have concluded him to be divinely assisted and commissioned, who without the help of education gave such proofs of extraordinary wisdom and power. <div eID="gen22364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22365" type="x-p"/> 2. The meanness and poverty of his relations, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.55-Matt.13.56">v. 55, 56</reference>. <div eID="gen22365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22366" type="x-p"/> (1.) They upbraid him with his father. <hi type="italic">Is not this the carpenter's son?</hi> Yes, it is true he was reputed so: and what harm in that? No disparagement to him to be the son of an honest tradesman. They remember not (though they might have known it) that this carpenter was <hi type="italic">of the house of David</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.27">Luke i. 27</reference>), <hi type="italic">a son of David</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.20">ch. i. 20</reference>); though a carpenter, yet a person of honour. Those who are willing to pick quarrels will overlook that which is worthy and deserving, and fasten upon that only which seems mean. Some sordid spirits regard no branch, no not the Branch from the stem of Jesse (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Isa. xi. 1</reference>), if it be not the top branch. <div eID="gen22366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22367" type="x-p"/> (2.) They upbraid him with his mother; and what quarrel have they with her? Why, truly, <hi type="italic">his mother is called Mary,</hi> and that was a very common name, and they all knew her, and knew her to be an ordinary person; she <hi type="italic">was called Mary,</hi> not <hi type="italic">Queen Mary,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">Lady Mary,</hi> nor so much as <hi type="italic">Mistress Mary,</hi> but plain <hi type="italic">Mary;</hi> and this is turned to his reproach, as if men had nothing to be valued by but foreign extraction, noble birth, or splendid titles; poor things to measure worth by. <div eID="gen22367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22368" type="x-p"/> (3.) They upbraid him with his brethren, whose names they knew, and had them ready enough to serve this turn; James, and Joses, and Simon, and Judas, good men but poor men, and therefore despised; and Christ for their sakes. These brethren, it is probable, were Joseph's children by a former wife; or whatever their relation was to him, they seem to have been brought up with him in the same family. And therefore of the calling of three of these, who were of the twelve, to that honour (James, Simon, and Jude, the same with Thaddeus), we read not particularly, because they needed not such an express call into acquaintance with Christ who had been the companions of his youth. <div eID="gen22368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22369" type="x-p"/> (4.) His sisters too are all with us; they should therefore have loved him and respected him the more, because he was one of themselves, but therefore they despised him. They were <hi type="italic">offended in him:</hi> they stumbled at these stumbling-stones, for he was set for <hi type="italic">a sign that should be spoken against,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.2.34">Luke ii. 34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.14">Isa. viii. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen22369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22370" type="x-p"/> II. See how he resented this contempt, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.57-Matt.13.58">v. 57, 58</reference>. <div eID="gen22370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22371" type="x-p"/> 1. It did not trouble his heart. It appears he was not much concerned at it; he <hi type="italic">despised the shame,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.2">Heb. xii. 2</reference>. Instead of aggravating the affront, or expressing an offence at it, or returning such an answer to their foolish suggestions as they deserved, he mildly imputes it to the common humour of the children of men, to undervalue excellences that are cheap, and common, and home-bred. It is usually so. <hi type="italic">A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country.</hi> Note, (1.) Prophets should have honour paid them, and commonly have; men of God are great men, and men of honour, and challenge respect. It is strange indeed if prophets have not honour. (2.) Notwithstanding this, they are commonly least regarded and reverenced in their own country, nay, and sometimes are most envied. Familiarity breeds contempt. <div eID="gen22371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22372" type="x-p"/> 2. It did for the present (to speak with reverence), in effect, tie his hands: <hi type="italic">He did not many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.</hi> Note, Unbelief is the great obstruction to Christ's favours. <hi type="italic">All things are</hi> in general <hi type="italic">possible to God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.26">ch. xix. 26</reference>), but then it is <hi type="italic">to him that believes</hi> as to the particulars, <reference osisRef="Mark.9.23">Mark ix. 23</reference>. The gospel is <hi type="italic">the power of God unto salvation,</hi> but then it is to <hi type="italic">every one that believes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.1.16">Rom. i. 16</reference>. So that if mighty works be not wrought in us, it is not for want of power or grace in Christ, but for want of faith in us. <hi type="italic">By grace ye are saved,</hi> and that is a mighty work, but it is <hi type="italic">through faith,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.8">Eph. ii. 8</reference>.  <chapter eID="Matt.13"/> <div eID="gen22372" type="x-p"/>

entries.bb61bcece2209d4a9ada0c18a13ab50377ca4f08: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13585"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 13</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.13.1-Matt.13.52">Mt 13:1-52</reference>. Jesus Teaches by Parables. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.4.1-Mark.4.34">Mr 4:1-34</reference>; Lu 8:4-18; 13:<reference osisRef="Luke.18.18-Luke.18.20">18-20</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen25996" type="x-p"/> Introduction (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.1-Matt.13.3">Mt 13:1-3</reference>).<div eID="gen25996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25997" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13585"/>1. The same day went Jesus out of the house, and sat by the seaside. <div eID="gen25997" type="x-p"/>
entries.6fc60117edaa863471ca558effe182a0b9321a67: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13586"/><div sID="gen25998" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13586"/><hi type="bold">2. And great multitudes were gathered together unto him, so that he went into a ship--</hi>the article in the received text lacks authority<div eID="gen25998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25999" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and sat; and the whole multitude stood on the shore--</hi>How graphic this picture!--no doubt from the pen of an eye-witness, himself impressed with the scene. It was "the same day" on which the foregoing solemn discourse was delivered, when His kindred thought Him "beside Himself" for His indifference to food and repose--that same day retiring to the seashore of Galilee; and there seating Himself, perhaps for coolness and rest, the crowds again flock around Him, and He is fain to push off from them, in the boat usually kept in readiness for Him; yet only to begin, without waiting to rest, a new course of teaching by parables to the eager multitudes that lined the shore. To the parables of our Lord there is nothing in all language to be compared, for simplicity, grace, fulness, and variety of spiritual teaching. They are adapted to all classes and stages of advancement, being understood by each according to the measure of his spiritual capacity. <div eID="gen25999" type="x-p"/>
entries.a29fdb59b9c5190b6437fa9b4ee3810450d38a6f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13587"/><div sID="gen26000" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13587"/><hi type="bold">3. And he spake many things unto them in parables, saying, &c.--</hi>These parables are SEVEN in number; and it is not a little remarkable that while this is the sacred number, the first FOUR of them were spoken to the mixed multitude, while the remaining THREE were spoken to the Twelve in private--these divisions, four and three, being themselves notable in the symbolical arithmetic of Scripture. Another thing remarkable in the structure of these parables is, that while the first of the Seven--that of the Sower--is of the nature of an Introduction to the whole, the remaining Six consist of three pairs--the Second and Seventh, the Third and Fourth, and the Fifth and Sixth, corresponding to each other; each pair setting forth the same general truths, but with a certain diversity of aspect. All this can hardly be accidental.<div eID="gen26000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26001" type="x-p"/> First Parable: The Sower (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.3-Matt.9.18">Mt 13:3-9, 18</reference>-<reference osisRef="Matt.9.23">23</reference>).<div eID="gen26001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26002" type="x-p"/> This parable may be entitled, The Effect of the Word Dependent on the State of the Heart. For the exposition of this parable, see on Mr 4:<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.14-1Cor.9.20">1-9, 14-20</reference>.<div eID="gen26002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26003" type="x-p"/> Reason for Teaching in Parables (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.10-Matt.13.17">Mt 13:10-17</reference>). <div eID="gen26003" type="x-p"/>
entries.b7e53d8d091d3138e48d48bf3ce1935863fb3807: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13588"/><div sID="gen26004" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13588"/><hi type="bold">10. And the disciples came, and said unto him--</hi>"they that were with Him, when they were alone" (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.10">Mr 4:10</reference>).<div eID="gen26004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26005" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Why speakest thou to them in parables?--</hi>Though before this He had couched some things in the parabolic form, for more vivid illustration, it would appear that He now, for the first time, formally employed this method of teaching. <div eID="gen26005" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd0ced748c7319f72abadf06659519bbe21f417d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13589"/><div sID="gen26006" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13589"/><hi type="bold">11. He answered and said unto them, Because it is given unto you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven--</hi>The word "mysteries" in Scripture is not used in its classical sense--of religious secrets, nor yet of things incomprehensible, or in their own nature difficult to be understood--but in the sense of things of purely divine revelation, and, usually, things darkly announced under the ancient economy, and during all that period darkly understood, but fully published under the Gospel (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.6-1Cor.2.10">1Co 2:6-10</reference>; Ep 3:3-6, 8, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.9">9</reference>). "The mysteries of the kingdom of heaven," then, mean those glorious Gospel truths which at that time only the more advanced disciples could appreciate, and they but partially.<div eID="gen26006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26007" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but to them it is not given--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.11.25">Mt 11:25</reference>). Parables serve the double purpose of revealing and concealing; presenting "the mysteries of the kingdom" to those who know and relish them, though in never so small a degree, in a new and attractive light; but to those who are insensible to spiritual things yielding only, as so many tales, some temporary entertainment. <div eID="gen26007" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9bcade8756451182e796a1aac120a6fe826c025: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13590"/><div sID="gen26008" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13590"/><hi type="bold">12. For whosoever hath--</hi>that is, keeps; as a thing which he values.<div eID="gen26008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26009" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to him shall be given, and he shall have more abundance--</hi>He will be rewarded by an increase of what he so much prizes.<div eID="gen26009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26010" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but whosoever hath not--</hi>who lets this go or lie unused, as a thing on which he sets no value.<div eID="gen26010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26011" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from him shall be taken away even that he hath--</hi>or as it is in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.18">Lu 8:18</reference>), "what he seemeth to have," or, thinketh he hath. This is a principle of immense importance, and, like other weighty sayings, appears to have been uttered by our Lord on more than one occasion, and in different connections. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.25.9">Mt 25:9</reference>). As a great ethical principle, we see it in operation everywhere, under the general law of habit; in virtue of which moral principles become stronger by exercise, while by disuse, or the exercise of their contraries, they wax weaker, and at length expire. The same principle reigns in the intellectual world, and even in the animal--if not in the vegetable also--as the facts of physiology sufficiently prove. Here, however, it is viewed as a divine ordination, as a judicial retribution in continual operation under the divine administration. <div eID="gen26011" type="x-p"/>
entries.9d4631e66922793fe4e837f774b878300951cff2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13591"/><div sID="gen26012" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13591"/><hi type="bold">13. Therefore speak I to them in parables--</hi>which our Lord, be it observed, did not begin to do till His miracles were malignantly ascribed to Satan.<div eID="gen26012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26013" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because they seeing, see not--</hi>They "saw," for the light shone on them as never light shone before; but they "saw not," for they closed their eyes.<div eID="gen26013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and hearing, they hear not; neither do they understand--</hi>They "heard," for He taught them who "spake as never man spake"; but they "heard not," for they took nothing in, apprehending not the soul-penetrating, life-giving words addressed to them. In Mark and Luke (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.12">Mr 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.8.10">Lu 8:10</reference>), what is here expressed as a human fact is represented as the fulfilment of a divine purpose--"that seeing they may see, and not perceive," &c. The explanation of this lies in the statement of the foregoing verse--that, by a fixed law of the divine administration, the duty men voluntarily refuse to do, and in point of fact do not do, they at length become morally incapable of doing. <div eID="gen26014" type="x-p"/>
entries.9263f56d1de9c3739edeee1f98f104dc152f3ed8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13592"/><div sID="gen26015" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13592"/><hi type="bold">14. And in them is fulfilled--</hi>rather, "is fulfilling," or "is receiving its fulfilment."<div eID="gen26015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26016" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the prophecy of Esaias, which saith--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.6.9">Is 6:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">10</reference>--here quoted according to the Septuagint).<div eID="gen26016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26017" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">By hearing ye shall hear, and shall not understand, &c.--</hi>They were thus judicially sealed up under the darkness and obduracy which they deliberately preferred to the light and healing which Jesus brought nigh to them. <div eID="gen26017" type="x-p"/>
entries.722f41ca238388e1a24c2e9b86aa2a0f88b78f69: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13593"/><div sID="gen26018" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13593"/><hi type="bold">16. But blessed are your eyes, for they see; and your cars, for they hear--</hi>that is, "Happy ye, whose eyes and ears, voluntarily and gladly opened, are drinking in the light divine." <div eID="gen26018" type="x-p"/>
entries.11c5829487fb4ee11b8f5b475aff534f25e8d932: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13594"/><div sID="gen26019" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13594"/><hi type="bold">17. For verily I say unto you, That many prophets and righteous men have desired--</hi>rather, "coveted."<div eID="gen26019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26020" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to see those things which ye see, and have not seen them; and to hear those things which ye hear, and have not heard them--</hi>Not only were the disciples blessed above the blinded just spoken of, but favored above the most honored and the best that lived under the old economy, who had but glimpses of the things of the new kingdom, just sufficient to kindle in them desires not to be fulfilled to any in their day. In <reference osisRef="Luke.10.23">Lu 10:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.10.24">24</reference>, where the same saying is repeated on the return of the Seventy--the words, instead of "many prophets and righteous men," are "many prophets and kings"; for several of the Old Testament saints were kings.<div eID="gen26020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26021" type="x-p"/> Second and Seventh Parables or First Pair:<div eID="gen26021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26022" type="x-p"/> The Wheat and the Tares, and The Good and Bad Fish (Mt 13:24-30, 36-43, 47-50).<div eID="gen26022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26023" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The subject of both these parables--</hi>which teach the same truth, with a slight diversity of aspect--is:<div eID="gen26023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26024" type="x-p"/> The MIXED CHARACTER OF THE Kingdom in Its Present State, and the FINAL ABSOLUTE SEPARATION OF THE Two Classes.<div eID="gen26024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26025" type="x-p"/> The Tares and the Wheat (Mt 13:24-30, 36-43).<div eID="gen26025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26026" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">24, 36-38. Another parable put he forth unto them, saying, The kingdom of heaven is likened unto a man which sowed good seed in his field--</hi>Happily for us, these exquisite parables are, with like charming simplicity and clearness, expounded to us by the Great Preacher Himself. Accordingly, we pass to: <reference osisRef="Matt.13.36-Matt.13.38">Mt 13:36-38</reference>. See on <reference osisRef="Matt.13.36">Mt 13:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.13.38">Mt 13:38</reference><div eID="gen26026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26027" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">25, 38, 39. But while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat, and went his way--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.13.38">Mt 13:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.39">39</reference>). <div eID="gen26027" type="x-p"/>
entries.85bcd0cb0b9aae81a3ea2009595c8435483faaa8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13595"/><div sID="gen26028" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13595"/><hi type="bold">26. But when the blade was sprung up, and brought forth fruit, then appeared the tares also--</hi>the growth in both cases running parallel, as antagonistic principles are seen to do. <div eID="gen26028" type="x-p"/>
entries.0bf76da70bc5e3c655ceec640e4a7b087d41722b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13596"/><div sID="gen26029" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13596"/><hi type="bold">27. So the servants of the householder came--</hi>that is, Christ's ministers.<div eID="gen26029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26030" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and said unto him, Sir, didst not thou sow good seed in thy field? from whence then hath it tares?--</hi>This well expresses the surprise, disappointment, and anxiety of Christ's faithful servants and people at the discovery of "false brethren" among the members of the Church. <div eID="gen26030" type="x-p"/>
entries.50afe06b1c28bfea920b727fd408b8ba2d746257: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13597"/><div sID="gen26031" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13597"/><hi type="bold">28. He said unto them, An enemy hath done this--</hi>Kind words these from a good Husbandman, honorably clearing His faithful servants of the wrong done to his field.<div eID="gen26031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26032" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The servants said unto him, Wilt thou then that we go and gather them up?--</hi>Compare with this the question of James and John (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.54">Lu 9:54</reference>), "Lord, wilt Thou that we command fire to come down from heaven and consume" those Samaritans? In this kind of zeal there is usually a large mixture of carnal heat. (See <reference osisRef="Jas.1.20">Jas 1:20</reference>). <div eID="gen26032" type="x-p"/>
entries.ef27b1ee57436de70f39af580fd8c11e00f4bcac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13598"/><div sID="gen26033" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13598"/><hi type="bold">29. But he said, Nay--</hi>"It will be done in due time, but not now, nor is it your business."<div eID="gen26033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26034" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lest, while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them--</hi>Nothing could more clearly or forcibly teach the difficulty of distinguishing the two classes, and the high probability that in the attempt to do so these will be confounded. <div eID="gen26034" type="x-p"/>
entries.e588de64dcfd4f285af93e941b83c3148b049e18: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13599"/><div sID="gen26035" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13599"/><hi type="bold">30-39. Let both grow together--</hi>that is, in the visible Church.<div eID="gen26035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26036" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">until the harvest--</hi>till the one have ripened for full salvation, the other for destruction. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.13.39">Mt 13:39</reference>).<div eID="gen26036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26037" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.13.39">Mt 13:39</reference>).<div eID="gen26037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26038" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them--</hi>"in the fire" (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.40">Mt 13:40</reference>).<div eID="gen26038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26039" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but gather the wheat into my barn--</hi>Christ, as the Judge, will separate the two classes (as in <reference osisRef="Matt.25.32">Mt 25:32</reference>). It will be observed that the tares are burned before the wheat is housed; in the exposition of the parable (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.41">Mt 13:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.43">43</reference>) the same order is observed: and the same in <reference osisRef="Matt.25.46">Mt 25:46</reference>--as if, in some literal sense, "with thine eyes shalt thou behold and see the reward of the wicked" (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.8">Psa 91:8</reference>).<div eID="gen26039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26040" type="x-p"/> Third and Fourth Parables or Second Pair:<div eID="gen26040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26041" type="x-p"/> The Mustard Seed and The Leaven (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.31-Matt.13.33">Mt 13:31-33</reference>).<div eID="gen26041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26042" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">The subject of both these parables, as of the first pair, is the same, but under a slight diversity of aspect, namely--</hi> <div eID="gen26042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26043" type="x-p"/> The GROWTH OF THE KINGDOM FROM THE Smallest Beginnings to Ultimate Universality.<div eID="gen26043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26044" type="x-p"/> The Mustard Seed (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.31">Mt 13:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.32">32</reference>). <div eID="gen26044" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a4ab1da4ea71d85f77a5dfccd99e07ba7d6d356: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13608"/><div sID="gen26059" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13608"/><hi type="bold">41. The Son of man shall send forth his angels, and they shall gather out of his kingdom--</hi>to which they never really belonged. They usurped their place and name and outward privileges; but "the ungodly shall not stand in the judgment, nor sinners [abide] in the congregation of the righteous" (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.5">Psa 1:5</reference>).<div eID="gen26059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26060" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all things that offend--</hi>all those who have proved a stumbling-block to others<div eID="gen26060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26061" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and them which do iniquity--</hi>The former class, as the worst, are mentioned first. <div eID="gen26061" type="x-p"/>
entries.10038f7d7aac9b864648462fcbbe21927cc8a42d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13609"/><div sID="gen26062" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13609"/><hi type="bold">42. And shall cast them into a furnace of fire--</hi>rather, "the furnace of fire":<div eID="gen26062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26063" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth--</hi>What terrific strength of language--the "casting" or "flinging" expressive of indignation, abhorrence, contempt (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.9.17">Psa 9:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Da 12:2</reference>): "the furnace of fire" denoting the fierceness of the torment: the "wailing" signifying the anguish this causes; while the "gnashing of teeth" is a graphic way of expressing the despair in which its remedilessness issues (see <reference osisRef="Matt.8.12">Mt 8:12</reference>)! <div eID="gen26063" type="x-p"/>
entries.92b8cb84cd8b39b86ce9bf4e5ce2b84555ce559e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13610"/><div sID="gen26064" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13610"/><hi type="bold">43. Then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father--</hi>as if they had been under a cloud during the present association with ungodly pretenders to their character, and claimants of their privileges, and obstructors of their course.<div eID="gen26064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26065" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Who hath ears to hear, let him hear--</hi>(See <reference osisRef="Mark.4.9">Mr 4:9</reference>).<div eID="gen26065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26066" type="x-p"/> Fifth and Sixth Parables or Third Pair: The Hidden Treasure and The Pearl of Great Price (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.44-Matt.13.46">Mt 13:44-46</reference>).<div eID="gen26066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26067" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">The subject of this last pair, as of the two former, is the same, but also under a slight diversity of aspect: namely--</hi> <div eID="gen26067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26068" type="x-p"/> The Priceless Value of the Blessings of the Kingdom. And while the one parable represents the Kingdom as "found without seeking," the other holds forth the Kingdom as "sought and found."<div eID="gen26068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26069" type="x-p"/> The Hidden Treasure (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.44">Mt 13:44</reference>). <div eID="gen26069" type="x-p"/>
entries.e711b9ba71a8bffc8882ef70d55d8936523d54bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13611"/><div sID="gen26070" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13611"/><hi type="bold">44. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field--</hi>no uncommon thing in unsettled and half-civilized countries, even now as well as in ancient times, when there was no other way of securing it from the rapacity of neighbors or marauders. (<reference osisRef="Jer.41.8">Jr 41:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.3.21">Job 3:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.2.4">Pr 2:4</reference>).<div eID="gen26070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the which when a man hath found--</hi>that is, unexpectedly found.<div eID="gen26071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26072" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he hideth, and for joy thereof--</hi>on perceiving what a treasure he had lighted on, surpassing the worth of all he possessed.<div eID="gen26072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26073" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field--</hi>in which case, by Jewish law, the treasure would become his own.<div eID="gen26073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26074" type="x-p"/> The Pearl of Great Price (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.45">Mt 13:45</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.46">46</reference>). <div eID="gen26074" type="x-p"/>
entries.f0b8a1fd2254e5842fda5233a9435426aeb0dcd3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13612"/><div sID="gen26075" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13612"/>45. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchantman, seeking goodly pearls. <div eID="gen26075" type="x-p"/>
entries.000982a5bd942b47c93c66af58ab1ae04cf992fc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13613"/><div sID="gen26076" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13613"/><hi type="bold">46. Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it--</hi>The one pearl of great price, instead of being found by accident, as in the former case, is found by one whose business it is to seek for such, and who finds it just in the way of searching for such treasures. But in both cases the surpassing value of the treasure is alike recognized, and in both all is parted with for it.<div eID="gen26076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26077" type="x-p"/> The Good and Bad Fish (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.47-Matt.13.50">Mt 13:47-50</reference>).<div eID="gen26077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26078" type="x-p"/> The object of this brief parable is the same as that of the Tares and Wheat. But as its details are fewer, so its teaching is less rich and varied. <div eID="gen26078" type="x-p"/>
entries.2bb00b3e571e6d995ac26120d92d21058f2dab33: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13614"/><div sID="gen26079" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13614"/><hi type="bold">47. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a net, that was cast into the sea, and gathered of every kind--</hi>The word here rendered "net" signifies a large drag-net, which draws everything after it, suffering nothing to escape, as distinguished from a casting-net (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.16">Mr 1:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.18">18</reference>). The far-reaching efficacy of the Gospel is thus denoted. This Gospel net "gathered of every kind," meaning every variety of character. <div eID="gen26079" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa1970dde11ef27bf116498667255baa878c833b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13615"/><div sID="gen26080" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13615"/><hi type="bold">48. Which, when it was full, they drew to shore--</hi>for the separation will not be made till the number of the elect is accomplished.<div eID="gen26080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26081" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and sat down--</hi>expressing the deliberateness with which the judicial separation will at length be made.<div eID="gen26081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26082" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and gathered the good into vessels, but cast the bad away--</hi>literally, "the rotten," but here meaning, "the foul" or "worthless" fish: corresponding to the "tares" of the other parable. <div eID="gen26082" type="x-p"/>
entries.e4cd0e07ca06360072d9f3cdaeb6635446edff23: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13616"/><div sID="gen26083" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13616"/><hi type="bold">49. So shall it be at the end of the world, &c.--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.13.42">Mt 13:42</reference>). We have said that each of these two parables holds forth the same truth under a slight diversity of aspect. What is that diversity? First, the bad, in the former parable, are represented as vile seed sown among the wheat by the enemy of souls; in the latter, as foul fish drawn forth out of the great sea of human beings by the Gospel net itself. Both are important truths--that the Gospel draws within its pale, and into the communion of the visible Church, multitudes who are Christians only in name; and that the injury thus done to the Church on earth is to be traced to the wicked one. But further, while the former parable gives chief prominence to the present mixture of good and bad, in the latter, the prominence is given to the future separation of the two classes. <div eID="gen26083" type="x-p"/>
entries.932eb8c66e8680f0fb02a44f496996164ab570a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13617"/><div sID="gen26084" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13617"/><hi type="bold">51. Jesus saith unto them--</hi>that is, to the Twelve. He had spoken the first four in the hearing of the mixed multitude: the last three He reserved till, on the dismissal of the mixed audience, He and the Twelve were alone (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.36">Mt 13:36</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen26084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26085" type="x-p"/> Have ye understood all these things? They say unto him, Yea, Lord. <div eID="gen26085" type="x-p"/>
entries.92f444570afbf6790aa085d78842e5af5a410cb1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13618"/><div sID="gen26086" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13618"/><hi type="bold">52. Then said he unto them, Therefore--</hi>or as we should say, "Well, then."<div eID="gen26086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26087" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every scribe--</hi>or Christian teacher: here so called from that well-known class among the Jews. (See <reference osisRef="Matt.23.34">Mt 23:34</reference>).<div eID="gen26087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26088" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven--</hi>himself taught in the mysteries of the Gospel which he has to teach to others.<div eID="gen26088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26089" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is like unto a man that is an householder which bringeth forth--</hi>"turneth" or "dealeth out."<div eID="gen26089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26090" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of his treasure--</hi>his store of divine truth.<div eID="gen26090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26091" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">things new and old--</hi>old truths in ever new forms, aspects, applications, and with ever new illustrations. <div eID="gen26091" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f3d148e54205a6c6dea907a564cb2a4aeb77323: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13619"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.13.53-Matt.13.58">Mt 13:53-58</reference>. How Jesus Was Regarded by His Relatives. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.6.1-Mark.6.6">Mr 6:1-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.4.16-Luke.4.30">Lu 4:16-30</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26092" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13619"/>53. And it came to pass, that, when Jesus had finished these parables, he departed thence. <div eID="gen26092" type="x-p"/>
entries.c7f3135ee2b2f766470b5c5e5c7f4baa1b7689f3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13620"/><div sID="gen26093" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13620"/><hi type="bold">54. And when he was come into his own country--</hi>that is, Nazareth; as is plain from <reference osisRef="Mark.6.1">Mr 6:1</reference>. See on <reference osisRef="John.4.43">Joh 4:43</reference>, where also the same phrase occurs. This, according to the majority of Harmonists, was the second of two visits which our Lord paid to Nazareth during His public ministry; but in our view it was His first and only visit to it. See on <reference osisRef="Matt.4.13">Mt 4:13</reference>; and for the reasons, see <reference osisRef="Luke.4.16-Luke.4.30">Lu 4:16-30</reference>.<div eID="gen26093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26094" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Whence hath this man this wisdom, and these mighty works?--</hi>"these miracles." These surely are not like the questions of people who had asked precisely the same questions before, who from astonishment had proceeded to rage, and in their rage had hurried Him out of the synagogue, and away to the brow of the hill whereon their city was built, to thrust Him down headlong, and who had been foiled even in that object by His passing through the midst of them, and going His way. But see on <reference osisRef="Luke.4.16">Lu 4:16</reference>, &c. <div eID="gen26094" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f6cc3e591fec4d08f0e1d60579386270979e872: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13621"/><div sID="gen26095" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13621"/><hi type="bold">55. Is not this the carpenter's son?--</hi>In Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.3">Mr 6:3</reference>) the question is, "Is not this the carpenter?" In all likelihood, our Lord, during His stay under the roof of His earthly parents, wrought along with His legal father.<div eID="gen26095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26096" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is not his mother called Mary?--</hi>"Do we not know all about His parentage? Has He not grown up in the midst of us? Are not all His relatives our own townsfolk? Whence, then, such wisdom and such miracles?" These particulars of our Lord's human history constitute the most valuable testimony, first, to His true and real humanity--for they prove that during all His first thirty years His townsmen had discovered nothing about Him different from other men; secondly, to the divine character of His mission--for these Nazarenes proclaim both the unparalleled character of His teaching and the reality and glory of His miracles, as transcending human ability; and thirdly, to His wonderful humility and self-denial--in that when He was such as they now saw Him to be, He yet never gave any indications of it for thirty years, because "His hour was not yet come."<div eID="gen26096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26097" type="x-p"/> And his brethren, James, and Joses, and Simon, and Judas? <div eID="gen26097" type="x-p"/>
entries.a63f9f7e41dbb6f48bb304464438471e6a782df1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13622"/><div sID="gen26098" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13622"/><hi type="bold">56. And his sisters, are they not all with us? Whence then hath this man all these things? An exceedingly difficult question here arises--</hi>What were these "brethren" and "sisters" to Jesus? Were they, First, His full brothers and sisters? or, Secondly, Were they His step-brothers and step-sisters, children of Joseph by a former marriage? or, Thirdly, Were they cousins, according to a common way of speaking among the Jews respecting persons of collateral descent? On this subject an immense deal has been written, nor are opinions yet by any means agreed. For the second opinion there is no ground but a vague tradition, arising probably from the wish for some such explanation. The first opinion undoubtedly suits the text best in all the places where the parties are certainly referred to (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.46">Mt 12:46</reference>; and its parallels, <reference osisRef="Mark.3.31">Mr 3:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.8.19">Lu 8:19</reference>; our present passage, and its parallels, <reference osisRef="Mark.6.3">Mr 6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.2.12">Joh 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.3">7:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.10">5, 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.14">Ac 1:14</reference>). But, in addition to other objections, many of the best interpreters, thinking it in the last degree improbable that our Lord, when hanging on the cross, would have committed His mother to John if He had had full brothers of His own then alive, prefer the third opinion; although, on the other hand, it is not to be doubted that our Lord might have good reasons for entrusting the guardianship of His doubly widowed mother to the beloved disciple in preference even to full brothers of His own. Thus dubiously we prefer to leave this vexed question, encompassed as it is with difficulties. As to the names here mentioned, the first of them, "James," is afterwards called "the Lord's brother" (see on <reference osisRef="Gal.1.19">Ga 1:19</reference>), but is perhaps not to be confounded with "James the son of Alphæus," one of the Twelve, though many think their identity beyond dispute. This question also is one of considerable difficulty, and not without importance; since the James who occupies so prominent a place in the Church of Jerusalem, in the latter part of the Acts, was apparently the apostle, but is by many regarded as "the Lord's brother," while others think their identity best suits all the statements. The second of those here named, "Joses" (or Joseph), must not be confounded with "Joseph called Barsabas, who was surnamed Justus" (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.23">Ac 1:23</reference>); and the third here named, "Simon," is not to be confounded with Simon the Kananite or Zealot (see on <reference osisRef="Matt.10.4">Mt 10:4</reference>). These three are nowhere else mentioned in the New Testament. The fourth and last-named, "Judas," can hardly be identical with the apostle of that name--though the brothers of both were of the name of "James"--nor (unless the two be identical, was this Judas) with the author of the catholic Epistle so called. <div eID="gen26098" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f9ed47cb4b5709ae5b19d64874de51c33092fda: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13623"/><div sID="gen26099" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13623"/><hi type="bold">58. And he did not many mighty works there, because of their unbelief--</hi>"save that He laid His hands on a few sick folk, and healed them" (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.5">Mr 6:5</reference>). See on <reference osisRef="Luke.4.16-Luke.4.30">Lu 4:16-30</reference>. <chapter eID="Matt.13"/>

entries.c8a02b55bc14a1360a970159c7078ed1ebe45049: <div eID="gen37316" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen37317" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen37318" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen37318" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen37317" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen37319" type="x-p"/> Christ teaches the multitudes out of a ship, they standing on the shore, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.1">Mat 13:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.2">Mat 13:2</reference>. The parable of the sower, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.3-Mat.13.9">Mat 13:3-9</reference>. He gives his reasons for speaking in parables, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.10-Mat.13.17">Mat 13:10-17</reference>. Explains the parable of the sower, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.18-Mat.13.23">Mat 13:18-23</reference>. Parable of the tares and the wheat, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.24-Mat.13.30">Mat 13:24-30</reference>. Of the grain of mustard seed, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.31">Mat 13:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.32">Mat 13:32</reference>. Of the leaven, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.33">Mat 13:33</reference>. The prophecy fulfilled by this mode of teaching, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.34">Mat 13:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.35">Mat 13:35</reference>. He explains the parable of the tares and the wheat, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.36-Mat.13.43">Mat 13:36-43</reference>. Parable of the treasure hid in a field, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.44">Mat 13:44</reference>. Of the pearl-merchant, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.45">Mat 13:45</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.46">Mat 13:46</reference>. Of the dragnet, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.47-Mat.13.50">Mat 13:47-50</reference>. His application of the whole, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.51">Mat 13:51</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.52">Mat 13:52</reference>. He teaches in his own country, and his neighbors take offense, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.53-Mat.13.56">Mat 13:53-56</reference>. Our Lord's observations on this, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.57">Mat 13:57</reference>. He works no miracle among them because of their unbelief, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.58">Mat 13:58</reference>. <div eID="gen37319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37320" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen37320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37321" type="x-p"/> The same day - Our Lord scarcely ever appears to take any rest: he is incessant in his labors, and instant in season and out of season; and in this he has left all his successors in the ministry an example, that they should follow his steps: for he who wishes to save souls will find few opportunities to rest. As Satan is going about as a roaring lion seeking whom he may devour, the messenger of God should imitate his diligence, that he may counteract his work. The gospels are journals of our Lord's life. <div eID="gen37321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37322" type="x-p"/> Went Jesus out of the house - This was the house of Peter.
