Meanwhile, let us not despond, but rise by faith against the pride of the world, till the Lord give us that astonishing display of his power, <note n="224"> <div sID="gen99280" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Iuques a ce que le Seigneur nous face sentir l’effect de cette vertu incomprehensible</foreign>;” — “till the Lord make us feel the effect of that incomprehensible power.”<div eID="gen99280" type="x-p"/> </note> of which he speaks in this passage.<div eID="gen99278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99281" type="x-p"/>The word <hi type="italic">leaven </hi>is sometimes taken in a bad sense, as when Christ warns them to<div eID="gen99281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99282" type="x-p"/>beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees, <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.16.11">Matthew 16:11</reference>;)<div eID="gen99282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99283" type="x-p"/>and when Paul says, that<div eID="gen99283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99284" type="x-p"/>a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump, <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.5.6">1 Corinthians 5:6</reference>.)<div eID="gen99284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99285" type="x-p"/>But here the term must be understood simply as applying to the present subject. As to the meaning of the phrase, <hi type="italic">the kingdom of God, and the kingdom of heaven,</hi> we have spoken on former occasions.<div eID="gen99285" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.31" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99275" osisID="Matt.13.31" type="section"/>
entries.d96c01587f657ea8ae9dc913f24445ab68f8aa90: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.34" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.13.34" sID="gen99288" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99289" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.13.34">Matthew 13:34</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">All these things Jesus spoke in parables. </hi>Though Mark expressly says, that Christ <hi type="italic">spoke the word to them as they were able to bear it, </hi>yet I think it probable that he continued to employ <hi type="italic">parables, </hi>not so much for the purpose of instruction, as to keep the attention of his hearers awake till a more convenient time. For why did he explain them familiarly to his disciples when they were apart? Was it because they were more slow of apprehension than the great body of the people? No; but because he wished to convey to them privately a knowledge of his meaning, and to allow others to remain in a state of suspense, till a fitter opportunity should arrive. These were only a sort of introduction to the Gospel, the full brightness and publication of which was delayed till the proper time.<div eID="gen99289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99290" type="x-p"/>There is an apparent contradiction between this statement of Matthew and the prediction of Isaiah, which was quoted a little before. But this is easily removed; for, though he withdrew the light of doctrine from the reprobate, yet this did not prevent him from accommodating himself to their capacity, so as to render them inexcusable. He therefore adopted a method of teaching which was proper and suitable to hearers, whom he knew to be not yet sufficiently prepared to receive instruction.<div eID="gen99290" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.34" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99288" osisID="Matt.13.34" type="section"/>
entries.582f633fd442768328af1cb82d6a8ca868c23b09: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.35" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.13.35" sID="gen99291" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99292" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">35.</hi> <hi type="italic">That it might be fulfilled</hi> Matthew does not mean, that the psalm, which he quotes, is a prediction which relates peculiarly to Christ, but that, as the majesty of the Spirit was displayed in the discourse of the Prophet, in the same manner was his power manifested in the discourse of Christ. The Prophet, when he is about to speak of God’s covenant, by which he adopted the seed of Abraham, of the benefits which he continued to bestow upon his people, and of the whole government of the Church, introduces his subject in lofty terms, <hi type="italic">I will open my mouth in parables, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.78.2">Psalm 78:2</reference>:) that is, “I will not speak of trifling matters, but will handle with becoming gravity subjects of the highest importance.” When he adds, <hi type="italic">I will utter dark sayings, </hi>the meaning is the same; such repetitions being very frequent in the Psalms. The Hebrew word <foreign xml:lang="he">משלים</foreign>, <hi type="italic">(Meshalim) </hi>signifies <hi type="italic">comparisons; </hi>and it came afterwards to be applied to “weighty sentences,” because <hi type="italic">comparisons </hi>generally impart beauty and energy to a discourse. The word <foreign xml:lang="he">חידות</foreign> <hi type="italic">(Chidoth) </hi>sometimes denotes <hi type="italic">“riddles,” </hi>and at other times, “short sayings.”<div eID="gen99292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99293" type="x-p"/>Now though Matthew seems to allude to the word <hi type="italic">parable, </hi>he undoubtedly means, that Christ spoke figuratively, in order that his very style, being more brilliant than ordinary discourse, might carry more weight and dignity. In short, he says that what is contained in the psalm was <hi type="italic">fulfilled; </hi>because the use of allegories and figures tended to show, that Christ was treating of the hidden mysteries of God, and to prevent his doctrine from being despised. Hence, too, we infer, that there was no inconsistency in the various objects which Christ had in view, when he spoke to the people in a dark manner. Though he intended to conceal from the reprobate what he was saying, yet he labored to make them feel, even in the midst of their amazement, that there was something heavenly and divine in his language. <note n="225"> <div sID="gen99294" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Car combien qu’il voulust parler en telle sorte que les reprouvez n’y entendissent rien, il a toutesfois tellement modere son style, qu’en leur stupidite ils ont senti que son parler avoit quelque vertu celeste et Divine</foreign>;” — “for, though he intended to speak in such a manner, that the reprobate might understand nothing of it, yet he was so regulated in his style that, amidst their stupidity, they felt that his manner of speaking had some Divine and heavenly power.”<div eID="gen99294" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen99293" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.35" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99291" osisID="Matt.13.35" type="section"/>
entries.b8ab6d2e31740c143d417d22ff41ae5df3a43eaf: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.37" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.13.37" sID="gen99232" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99233" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">37. </hi><hi type="italic">He that soweth the good seed</hi> He had formerly said that <hi type="italic">the kingdom of heaven resembles a man sowing.</hi> The mode of expression is unusual, but plainly means, that the same thing happens with the preaching of the Gospel as usually takes place in the sowing of fields; <hi type="italic">the tares grow, up along with the wheat</hi> One peculiarity, however, is pointed out by him, when he says that the sowing of tares in the field was effected by the trick of <hi type="italic">an enemy. </hi>This is intended to inform us that, when many wicked men are mingled with believers, this is no accidental or natural occurrence, as if they were the same seed, but that we must learn to charge the blame of this evil on the devil. Not that, by condemning him, men are acquitted of guilt; but, in the first place, that no blame whatever may be laid on God on account of this fault which arose from the agency of another; and, secondly, that we may not be surprised to find <hi type="italic">tares </hi>frequently growing in the Lord’s field, since Satan is always on the watch to do mischief. Again, when Christ says, not that the ministers of the word sow, but that he alone sows, this is not without meaning; for though this cannot be supposed to be restricted to his person, yet as he makes use of our exertions, and employs us as his instruments, for cultivating his field, so that He alone acts by us and in us, he justly claims for himself what is, in some respects, common to his ministers. Let us, therefore, remember, that the Gospel is preached, not only by Christ’s command, but by his authority. and direction; in short, that we are only his hand, and that He alone is the Author of the work.<div eID="gen99233" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.37" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99232" osisID="Matt.13.37" type="section"/>
entries.9cceb15c240cd9426f97f6e39b043d8cbebf0601: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.39" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.13.39" sID="gen99234" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99235" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">39. </hi><hi type="italic">The harvest is the end of the world.</hi> This is, no doubt, a very distressing consideration, that the Church is burdened with the reprobate to the very <hi type="italic">end of the world;</hi> but Christ enjoins on us to exercise patience till that time, that we may not deceive ourselves with a vain hope. Pastors ought to labor strenuously to purify the Church; and all the godly, so far as their respective callings enable them, ought to lend assistance in this matter; but when all shall have devoted their united exertions to the general advantage, they will not succeed in such a manner as to purify the Church entirely from every defilement. Let us therefore hold, that nothing was farther from the design of Christ than to encourage pollution by lending countenance to it. All that he intended was, to exhort those who believed in him not to lose courage, because they are under the necessity of retaining wicked men among them; and, next, to restrain and moderate the zeal of those who fancy that they are not at liberty to join in a society with any but pure angels. <note n="212"> <div sID="gen99236" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Qui ne pensent point qu’il soit bon de s’adioindre a la compagnie des fideles, sinon que tout y soit pur comme entre les Anges</foreign>;”— “who do not think that it is proper to join themselves to the society of believers, unless every thing in it be as pure as among the Angels.”<div eID="gen99236" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen99235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99237" type="x-p"/>This passage has been most improperly abused by the Anabaptists, and by others like them, <note n="213"> <div sID="gen99238" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et semblables reveurs</foreign>;” — “and similar dreamers.”<div eID="gen99238" type="x-p"/> </note> to take from the Church the power of the sword. But it is easy to refute them; for since they approve of excommunication, which cuts off, at least for a time, the bad and reprobate, why may not godly magistrates, when necessity calls for it, use the sword against wicked men? They reply that, when the punishment is not capital, <note n="214"> <div sID="gen99239" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Quand la peine n’est pas a mort (comme est l’excommunication</foreign>;)” — “when the punishment, as in the case of excommunication, is not to death.”<div eID="gen99239" type="x-p"/> </note> there is room allowed for repentance; as if the thief on the cross (<reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.23.42">Luke 23:42</reference>) did not find the means of salvation. I shall satisfy myself with replying, that Christ does not now speak of the office of pastors or of magistrates, but removes the offense which is apt to disturb weak minds, when they perceive that the Church is composed not only of the elect, but of the polluted dregs of society.<div eID="gen99237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99240" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The reapers are the angels.</hi> This term must be viewed in reference to the present subject. In another passage, the Apostles are called <hi type="italic">reapers, </hi>as compared with the Prophets, because they have <hi type="italic">entered into their labors, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:John.4.38">John 4:38</reference>,) and it is enjoined on all the ministers of the word,<div eID="gen99240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99241" type="x-p"/>that they should bring forth fruit, and that their fruit should remain, <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.15.16">John 15:16</reference>.)<div eID="gen99241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99242" type="x-p"/>Such also is the import of that statement, that <hi type="italic">the fields are white, </hi>and are in want of reapers, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.4.35">John 4:35</reference>;) and again, that<div eID="gen99242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99243" type="x-p"/>the harvest is abundant, but the laborers are few, <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.9.37">Matthew 9:37</reference>.)<div eID="gen99243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99244" type="x-p"/>But here the comparison is applied in a different manner; for those who occupy a place in the Church are said to be planted in the Lord’s field. Nor is this inconsistent with what is said elsewhere, that Christ, as soon as he comes forth with his Gospel,<div eID="gen99244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99245" type="x-p"/>hath a winnowing-fan in his hand, and will thoroughly <lb/> cleanse his thrashing-floor, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.12">Matthew 3:12</reference>.)<div eID="gen99245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99246" type="x-p"/>These words describe the commencement of that cleansing, which, this passage declares, will not take place before the last day, because not till then will it be fully completed. Christ will put the last hand to the cleansing of the Church by means of <hi type="italic">angels, </hi>but he now begins to do the work by means of pious teachers. He assigns this office to <hi type="italic">angels, </hi>because they will not remain idle spectators before his tribunal, <note n="215"> <div sID="gen99247" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Devant le siege iudicial de sa maieste</foreign>;” — “before the judgment- seat of his majesty.”<div eID="gen99247" type="x-p"/> </note> but will hold themselves in readiness to execute his commands. It follows, that those who proceed, with undue haste, to root out whatever displeases them, prevent, as far as lies in their power, the sentence of Christ, deprive <hi type="italic">angels </hi>of their office, and rashly take that office on themselves.<div eID="gen99246" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.39" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99234" osisID="Matt.13.39" type="section"/>
entries.4816e1469f70f786850cccc63b963a8781fc3c0e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.41" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.13.41" sID="gen99248" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99249" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">41.</hi> <hi type="italic">They shall gather out of his kingdom all stumbling-blocks</hi> The words that follow, <hi type="italic">and those who commit iniquity, </hi>are added for the sake of exposition; for it is not intended to point out two different things, but to state, that then will be the full and seasonable time, when all things shall be restored to regular order, and when the <hi type="italic">wicked </hi>shall be removed, who are now <hi type="italic">stumbling-blocks.</hi> They are so called, because not only are their own lives wicked, but they undermine the faith of many, retard others in the right course, draw some entirely aside, and drive others headlong. We ought to draw from this a useful admonition, not to become indolent and careless on account of our being surrounded by so many <hi type="italic">stumbling-blocks, </hi>but to be zealous and active in guarding against them. It reproves also the effeminacy of those who are so delicate, that the smallest possible <hi type="italic">stumbling-blocks</hi> make them turn back. <note n="216"> <div sID="gen99250" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ils tournent incontinent bride</foreign>;” — “they immediately wheel about.”<div eID="gen99250" type="x-p"/> </note> It is difficult, I admit, not to stumble frequently, and even sometimes to fall, when <hi type="italic">stumbling-blocks</hi> without number lie across our path. But our minds ought to be fortified with confidence; for the Son of God, who commands his followers to walk in the midst of <hi type="italic">stumbling-blocks,</hi> will unquestionably give us strength to overcome them all. He pronounces likewise an awful punishment against any hypocrites and reprobate persons, who now appear to be the most distinguished citizens of the Church.<div eID="gen99249" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.41" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99248" osisID="Matt.13.41" type="section"/>
entries.8bc5eb2efc469e80979e1bab5a1a510c64461b17:
42. And shall cast them into a furnace of fire. This is a metaphorical expression; for, as the infinite glory which is laid up for the sons of God so far exceeds all our senses, that we cannot find words to express it, so the punishment which awaits the reprobate is incomprehensible, and is therefore shadowed out according to the measure of our capacity. From ignorance of this, the Sophists have tortured themselves, to no purpose, by fruitless disputes, as we have already hinted on a former occasion.
Harmony, volume 1 p. 200.
Some commentators, I am aware, carry their ingenious inquiries into every minute phrase; but as there is reason to fear that subtleties, which rest on no solid grounds, may lead us into idle fooleries, I choose to philosophize more sparingly, and to rest satisfied with the plain and natural meaning. If we put a question to those who are so delighted with matters of curiosity, how it comes about that, while Christ is asleep, and unacquainted with the affair, the devil sows tares among the good seed, they will have nothing to reply; but while I desire to exercise caution, I have endeavored to leave out nothing that is useful and necessary to be known.
entries.a863afef78154a1757d93665f8d49388719da40c:
43. Then will the righteous shine. What a remarkable consolation! The sons of God, who now lie covered with dust, or are held in no estimation, or even are loaded with reproaches, will then shine in full brightness, as when the sky is serene, and every cloud has been dispelled. The adverb then (τότε) is emphatic; for it contains an implied contrast between their present state and the ultimate restoration, by the expectation of which Christ animates those who believe in him. The meaning therefore is, Though many wicked men now hold a high rank in the Church, yet that blessed day is assuredly to be expected, when the Son of God shall raise his followers on high, and remove every thing that now tends to dim or conceal their brightness. It is no doubt true, that the future glory is promised to none but those in whom the image of God already shines, and who are transformed into it by continued advances of glory. But as the life of the godly is now hidden, and as their salvation is invisible, because it consists in hope, Christ properly directs the attention of believers to heaven, where they will find the glory that is promised to them.
In order to make a deeper impression on his hearers, our Lord unquestionably refers here to a passage in Daniel, (12:3,)
And they that are wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament.
“The Prophet,” he seems to say, “when he predicts a future brightness, intimates also that there is a temporary obscurity: and so, if we admit the prediction, we ought to endure patiently that mixture which, for a time, classes the elect of God with the reprobate.” By comparing this glory to the sun, he does not determine that it will be alike in all. As Christ now distributes his gifts variously
“Diversement, aux uns plus, aux autres moins;” — “variously, to some more, to others less.”
among believers, in like manner will he crown these gifts at the last day. But we must recollect what I have said, that the restoration, which is delayed till the last coming of Christ, is compared with the cloudy state of the world.
“Avec l’estat present du monde, qui est comme tout obscurci de brouillars;” — “with the present state of the world, which is entirely, so to speak, obscured by mists.”
The kingdom of the Father, as the inheritance of the godly, is contrasted with the earth, to remind them that here they are pilgrims, and therefore ought to look upwards towards heaven. In another passage, the kingdom of God is said to be within us, (Luke 17:21,) but we shall not obtain the full enjoyment of it till God be all in all, (1 Corinthians 15:28.)
Matthew 13:31-35; Mark 4:26-34; Luke 13:18-22
Matthew 13:31-35
Mark 4:26-34
Luke 13:18-22
31. He delivered another parable to them, saying, The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard, which a man took and sowed in his field: 32. Which indeed is the least of all seeds: but when it is grown up, it is the largest among herbs,
“Il est plus grand que les autres herbes;” — “it is larger than the other herbs.”
and becometh a tree, so that the fowls of heaven come and make their nests among its branches. 33. He spake another parable to them: The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid among three measures of meal, till the whole was leavenened. 34. All these things Jesus spoke in parables to the multitudes, and without a parable he spoke nothing to them. 35. That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, who saith, I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things which have been hidden from the foundation of the world.
 
26. And he said, The kingdom of God is as if a man should cast seed into the ground, 27. And sleep, and rise by night and day, and the corn should spring and grow up, while knoweth not how. 28. For the earth yieldeth fruit of itself, first the blade, then the ear, and then the full corn in the ear. 29. And when the fruit is matured, he immediately applieth the sickle, because the harvest is at hand. 30. And he said, To what shall we say that the kingdom of God is like? or with what comparison shall we compare it? 31. As a grain of mustard, which, when it is sown in the earth, is smaller than all the seeds which are in the earth; 32. And when it is sown, it springs up, and is larger than all herbs,
“Que toute autre herbe;” — “than every other herb.”
and putteth forth great branches, so that the fowls of heaven can make their nests under its shadow. 33. And by such parables he spake the word to them, as they were able to bear it: 34. But without a parable he did not speak to them, but he explained all things to his disciples when they were apart.
18. Therefore he said, To what is the kingdom of God like? and to what shall I compare it? 19. It is like a grain of mustard, which a man took and cast into his garden, and it grew, and became a large tree, and the fowls of the air made their nests among its branches. 20. And again he said, To what shall I compare the kingdom of God? 21. It is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened. 22. And he went through the cities and villages, teaching and journeying towards Jerusalem.
entries.a8d172a3b74927b85e29c0211c4f5b574f696cb0: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.44" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.13.44" sID="gen99308" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99309" type="x-p"/>The first two of these parables are intended to instruct believers to prefer <hi type="italic">the Kingdom of heaven</hi> to the whole world, and therefore to deny themselves and all the desires of the flesh, that nothing may prevent them from obtaining so valuable a possession. We are greatly in need of such a warning; for we are so captivated by the allurements of the world, that eternal life fades from our view; <note n="232"> <div sID="gen99310" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que nous venons a oublier la vie eternelle</foreign>;” — “that we come to forget eternal life.”<div eID="gen99310" type="x-p"/> </note> and in consequence of our carnality, the spiritual graces of God are far from being held by us in the estimation which they deserve. Justly, therefore, does Christ speak in such lofty terms of the excellence of eternal life, that we ought not to feel uneasiness at relinquishing, on account of it, whatever we reckon in other respects to be valuable.<div eID="gen99309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99311" type="x-p"/>First, he says, that <hi type="italic">the kingdom of heaven is like a hidden treasure.</hi> We commonly set a high value on what is visible, and therefore the new and spiritual life, which is held out to us in the Gospel, is little esteemed by us, because it is <hi type="italic">hidden, </hi>and lies in hope. There is the highest appropriateness in comparing it to <hi type="italic">a treasure, </hi>the value of which is in no degree diminished, though it may be buried in the earth, and withdrawn from the eyes of men. These words teach us, that we ought not to estimate the riches of the grace of God according to the views of our flesh, or according to their outward display, but in the same manner as a <hi type="italic">treasure, </hi>though it be <hi type="italic">hidden, </hi>is preferred to a vain appearance of wealth. The same instruction is conveyed by the other parable<hi type="italic">. One pearl,</hi> though it be small, is so highly valued, that a skillful <hi type="italic">merchant </hi>does not hesitate to <hi type="italic">sell </hi>houses and lands in order to purchase it. The excellence of the heavenly life is not perceived, indeed, by the sense of the flesh; and yet we do not esteem it according to its real worth, unless we are prepared to deny, on account of it, all that glitters in our eyes.<div eID="gen99311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99312" type="x-p"/>We now perceive the leading object of both parables. It is to inform us, that none are qualified for receiving the grace of the Gospel but those who disregard all other desires, and devote all their exertions, and all their faculties, to obtain it. It deserves our attention, also, that Christ does not pronounce the <hi type="italic">hidden treasure, </hi>or the <hi type="italic">pearl, </hi>to be so highly valued by all. The <hi type="italic">treasure</hi> is ascertained to be valuable, after that it has been <hi type="italic">found </hi>and known; and it is the skillful <hi type="italic">merchant </hi>that forms such an opinion about the <hi type="italic">pearl</hi> <note n="233"> <div sID="gen99313" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">C’est le bon <hi type="italic">marchand </hi>qui fait telle estime de la <hi type="italic">perle</hi></foreign>;” — “it is the good <hi type="italic">merchant </hi>who sets so high a value on the <hi type="italic">pearl.”</hi><div eID="gen99313" type="x-p"/> </note> These words denote the knowledge of faith. “The heavenly kingdom,” Christ tells us, “is commonly held as of no account, because men are incapable of relishing it, and do not perceive the inestimable value of that treasure which the Lord offers to us in the Gospel.”<div eID="gen99312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99314" type="x-p"/>But it is asked, is it necessary that we abandon every other possession, in order that we may enjoy eternal life? I answer briefly. The natural meaning of the words is, that the Gospel does not receive from us the respect which it deserves, unless we prefer it to all the riches, pleasures, honors, and advantages of the world, and to such an extent, that we are satisfied with the spiritual blessings which it promises, and throw aside every thing that would keep us from enjoying them; for those who aspire to heaven must be disengaged from every thing that would retard their progress. Christ exhorts those who believe in him to deny those things only which are injurious to godliness; and, at the same time, permits them to use and enjoy God’s temporal favors, as if they did not use them.<div eID="gen99314" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.44" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99308" osisID="Matt.13.44" type="section"/>
entries.0df6adc1974ab1a952d852f49494316da22e81c7: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.46" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.13.46" sID="gen99315" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99316" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">46. </hi><hi type="italic">And bought it.</hi> By the word <hi type="italic">buy </hi>Christ does not mean, that men bring any price, with which they may purchase for themselves the heavenly life; for we know on what condition the Lord invites believers in the book of Isaiah, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.55.1">55:1</reference>,) <hi type="italic">Come and buy wine and milk without money and without price. </hi>But though the heavenly life, and every thing that belongs to it, is the free gift of God, yet we are said to <hi type="italic">buy </hi>it, when we cheerfully relinquish the desires of the flesh, that nothing may prevent us from obtaining it; as Paul says, that he<div eID="gen99316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99317" type="x-p"/>reckoned all things to be loss and dung, that he might gain Christ, <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Phil.3.8">Philippians 3:8</reference>.)<div eID="gen99317" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.46" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99315" osisID="Matt.13.46" type="section"/>
entries.57a5a3cf9a521385678a4d0887574528c46fe41b: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.47" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.13.47" sID="gen99318" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99319" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">47. </hi><hi type="italic">Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net.</hi> No new instruction is here given by Christ; but what he formerly taught is confirmed by another parable, that the Church of God, so long as it exists in the world, is a mixture of the good with the bad, and is never free from stains and pollutions. And yet the design of this parable is perhaps different. It may be that Christ intends not only to remove the offense which perplexes many weak minds, because they do not find in the world all the purity that might be desired, but likewise to employ the influence of fear and modesty, in restraining his disciples from delighting themselves with the empty title, or mere profession, of faith. For my own part, I cheerfully adopt both views. Christ informs us, that a mixture of the good and the bad must be patiently endured till <hi type="italic">the end of the word; </hi>because, till that time, a true and perfect restoration of the Church will not take place. Again, he warns us, that it is not enough, and—what is more—that it is of little consequence to us, to be gathered into the fold, unless we are his true and chosen sheep. To this effect is the saying of Paul,<div eID="gen99319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99320" type="x-p"/>The Lord knoweth who are his; and let every one that calleth on the name of the Lord depart from iniquity, <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Tim.2.19">2 Timothy 2:19</reference>.)<div eID="gen99320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99321" type="x-p"/>The preaching of the Gospel is justly compared to a <hi type="italic">net </hi>sunk beneath the water, to inform us that the present state of the Church is confused.<div eID="gen99321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99322" type="x-p"/>Our God is the God of order, and not of confusion, <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.14.33">1 Corinthians 14:33</reference>,)<div eID="gen99322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99323" type="x-p"/>and, therefore, recommends to us discipline; but he permits hypocrites to remain for a time among believers, till the last day, when he will bring his kingdom to a state of perfection. So far as lies in our power, let us endeavor to correct vices, and let us exercise severity in removing pollutions; but the Church will not be free from every spot and blemish, until Christ shall have <hi type="italic">separated the sheep from the goats, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.25.32">Matthew 25:32</reference>.)<div eID="gen99323" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.47" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99318" osisID="Matt.13.47" type="section"/>
entries.3270c7ef755c725fd05cb426cfbd0bccd0bcc24a:
51. Have you understood all these things? We must keep in recollection what we have formerly seen, that all the parables of Christ were explained in private. And now the Lord, after having taught them in this kind and familiar manner, warns them at the same time, that his object, in taking so much pains to instruct them, was not merely that they might be well informed,
“Qu’ils gardent ceste cognoissance pour eux-mesmes seulement;” — “that they may keep that knowledge for themselves only.”
but that they might communicate to others what they had received. In this way he whets and excites their minds more and more to desire instruction. He says that teachers are like householders, who are not only careful about their own food, but have a store laid up for the nourishment of others; and who do not live at ease as to the passing day, but make provision for a future and distant period. The meaning, therefore, is, that the teachers of the Church ought to be prepared by long study for giving to the people, as out of a storehouse,
“Commoe nous voyons que le pere de famille tire de son cellier ou grenier toutes sortes de provisions;” — “as we see that the master of a family draws from his cellar or granary all kinds of provisions.”
a variety of instruction concerning the word of God, as the necessity of the case may require. Many of the ancient expositors understand by things new and old the Law and the Gospel; but this appears to me to be forced. I understand them simply to mean a varied and manifold distribution, wisely and properly adapted to the capacity of every individual.
LUKE 7:36-50
Luke 7:36-50
36. And one of the Pharisees requested him to take food with him; and he entered into the house of the Pharisee, and sat down at table. 37. And, lo, a woman in the city, who was a sinner, when she knew that he sat at table in the house of the Pharisee, brought an alabaster box of ointment:
“Or voyci il y avoit une femme de la ville qui avoit este de mauvaise vie, laquelle ayant cognu qu’il estoit assis a table en la maison du Pharisien, apporta une boiste d’ongnement;” — “but, lo, there was a woman of the city who was of wicked life, who, having learned that he sat at table in the house of the Pharisee, brought a box of ointment.”
38. And sitting at his feet behind him, and weeping, she began to wash his feet with tears, and wiped them with the hairs of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with ointment.
“Et les frottoit d’ongnement;” — “and rubbed them with ointment.”
39. And the Pharisee, who had invited him, seeing it, said, speaking within himself, If this man were a Prophet, he would certainly know who and what sort of woman this is that toucheth him; for she is a sinner.
“Car elle est de mauvaise vie;” — “for she is of wicked life.”
40. And Jesus answering, said to him, Simon, I have something to say to thee. And he said, Master, say on. 41. A certain creditor had two debtors: one owed five hundred pence, and another fifty. 42. And when they had nothing to pay, he forgave them both. Tell me then, which of them will love him more? 43. Simon answering said, I suppose that it will be he to whom he forgave more. And he said to him, Thou hast decided aright. 44. And turning to the woman, he said to Simon, Seest thou this woman? I entered into thy house, thou gavest not water for my feet; but she hath moistened my feet with tears, and wiped them with the hairs of her head. 45. Thou gavest me not a kiss; but she, since the time that I entered, hath not ceased to kiss my feet. 47. For which reason I say to thee, Her many sins are forgiven, for she hath loved much; but he to whom less is forgiven loveth less. 48. And he said to her, Thy sins are forgiven thee. 49. And those who sat at table with him began to say within themselves, Who is this that even forgiveth sins? 50. And he said to the woman, Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace.
entries.4260015a82f0e12afd608ca48a10985c6be745bc: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.53" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.13.53" sID="gen99785" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99786" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.13.53">Matthew 13:53</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">When Jesus had concluded. Matthew </hi>does not mean, that immediately after delivering these discourses, he came into his own country; for it is evident from <hi type="italic">Mark, </hi>that some interval of time elapsed. But the meaning is, that after having taught for some time in Judea, he returned again to the Galileans, but did not receive from them kind treatment. A narrative which Luke gives (<reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.4.22">4:22</reference>) is nearly similar, but is not the same. Nor ought we to wonder that Christ’s countrymen, when they perceived that his family was mean and despised, and that he had been poorly educated, were at first so much offended as to murmur at his doctrine, and afterwards persevered in the same malice to such an extent, that they did not cease to slander him, when he chose to discharge the office of a prophet amongst them. This second rejection of Christ shows that the space of time which had intervened had not effected a reformation on the inhabitants of Nazareth, but that the same contempt was constantly thrown as an obstacle in the way, to prevent them from hearing Christ. <note n="345"> <div sID="gen99787" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">A fin de n’approcher de luy, et de ne recevoir sa doctrine</foreign>;” — “that they might not approach to him, and might not receive his doctrine.”<div eID="gen99787" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen99786" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.53" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99785" osisID="Matt.13.53" type="section"/>
entries.cf9b930d455e2e2ae8414bb31cc4b2f9c81af007: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.54" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.13.54" sID="gen99788" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99789" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">54.</hi> <hi type="italic">So that they were amazed.</hi> They are struck with <hi type="italic">amazement </hi>at the novelty of the occurrence, that Christ, who had not learned letters, but had been employed from youth to manhood in a mechanical occupation, is so eminent a teacher, and is filled with divine wisdom. In this miracle they ought to have perceived the hand of God; but their ingratitude made them cover themselves with darkness. <note n="346"> <div sID="gen99790" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mais par leur ingratitude ils se sont eblouis l’entendement, a fin de ne faire leur profit de ce qu’ils voyoyent devant leurs yeux</foreign>;” — “but by their ingratitude their understanding was dazzled, so that they did not derive advantage from what they saw before their eyes.”<div eID="gen99790" type="x-p"/> </note> They are compelled to admire him, whether they will or not; and yet they treat him with contempt. And what is this but to reject a prophet whom God has taught, because he has not been educated by men? They cut their throat by means of their own acknowledgment, when they render so honorable a testimony to the doctrine of Christ, which after all has no influence on them, because it does not take its origin, in the usual way, from the earth. Why do they not rather lift their eyes to heaven, and learn that what exceeds human reason must have come from God?<div eID="gen99789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99791" type="x-p"/>Besides, the miracles, which were added to the doctrine, ought to have affected them the more powerfully, or at least to have aroused them from their excessive carelessness and stupidity to glorify God; for certainly, when God adopts unwonted methods of procedure, so much the more clearly does he display the power of his hand. And yet this was the very reason why the inhabitants of Nazareth maliciously drew a veil over their eyes. We see, then, that it is not mere ignorance that hinders men, but that, of their own accord, they search after grounds of offense, to prevent them from following the path to which God invites. We ought rather to argue in the opposite way, that, when human means fail, the power of God is clearly revealed to us, and ought to receive undivided praise.<div eID="gen99791" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.54" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99788" osisID="Matt.13.54" type="section"/>
entries.b690608fa0c7e8428ee17e23f808644f491221f4:
55. Is not this the carpenter’s son? It was, we are aware, by the wonderful purpose of God, that Christ remained in private life till he was thirty years of age. Most improperly and unjustly, therefore, were the inhabitants of Nazareth offended on this account; for they ought rather to have received him with reverence, as one who had suddenly come down from heaven. They see God working in Christ, and intentionally turn away their eyes from this sight, to behold Joseph, and Mary, and all his relatives; thus interposing a veil to shut out the clearest light. The word brothers, we have formerly mentioned, is employed, agreeably to the Hebrew idiom, to denote any relatives whatever; and, accordingly, Helvidius displayed excessive ignorance in concluding that Mary must have had many sons, because Christ’s brothers are sometimes mentioned.
Jerome replied to Helvidius in a work entitled, Contra Helvidium de Beatoe Marioe Virginitate CAVIN has formerly alluded to the controversy between these two authors, (Harmony, vol. 1. p. 107.) — Ed.
entries.9b2a76a0433502dd006464b3607fb48f15d81645: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.57" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.13.57" sID="gen99795" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99796" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">57.</hi> <hi type="italic">A prophet is not devoid of honor.</hi> I have explained this statement at considerable length, where it occurs in the Gospel of John, <note n="348"> <div sID="gen99797" type="x-p"/> Our Author’s Preface to his Commentary on John’s Gospel is dated 1st January 1553; while the Preface to the Harmony is dated 1st August 1555. This accounts for the former being always referred to as an earlier work. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen99797" type="x-p"/> </note> (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.4.44">4:44</reference>.) It may, no doubt, be a general proverb, that those who are distinguished by eminent gifts are nowhere held in less estimation than <hi type="italic">in their own country; </hi>and this manifests the ingratitude of men, who, in proportion to the greater familiarity with which God exhibits himself to them, are the more bold to reject him in the influences of his Spirit. I readily agree, however, with Chrysostom, who thinks that this proverb was applied in a peculiar manner to the Jews. But what was usually spoken against the whole nation, Christ now asserts with special reference to his Galilean countrymen; for nowhere did he receive less honor than on his native soil. There were good grounds for the charge which he brings against them, that, instead of being the first to accept the grace offered to them, as they ought to have been, they drive him to a distance from them; for it is truly extraordinary that a prophet of God, whom others warmly receive as a newly-arrived stranger, should be despised in the place where he was born.<div eID="gen99796" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.13.57" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99795" osisID="Matt.13.57" type="section"/>

58. And he did not perform many miracles in that place. Mark states it more emphatically, that he could not perform any miracle. But they are perfectly agreed as to the substance of what is said, that it was the impiety of Christ’s countrymen that closed the door against the performance of a greater number of miracles among them. He had already given them some taste of his power; but they willingly stupify themselves, so as to have no relish for it. Accordingly, Augustine justly compares faith to the open mouth of a vessel, while he speaks of faith as resembling a stopper, by which the vessel is closed, so as not to receive the liquor
“La bonne liqueur;” — “the good liquor.”
which God pours into it. And undoubtedly this is the case; for when the Lord perceives that his power is not accepted by us, he at length withdraws it; and yet we complain that we are deprived of his aid, which our unbelief rejects and drives far from us.
When Mark declares that Christ could not perform any miracles, he represents the aggravated guilt of those by whom his goodness was prevented; for certainly unbelievers, as far as lies in their power, bind up the hands of God by their obstinacy; not that God is overcome, as if he were an inferior, but because they do not permit him to display his power. We must observe, however, what Mark adds, that some sick people, notwithstanding, were cured; for hence we infer, that the goodness of Christ strove with their malice, and triumphed over every obstacle.
“En sorte que quelques empeschemens qu’ils ayent scen y mettre, encore est—elle venue au dessus, et s’est monstree en quelque maniere.” —”So that, whatever obstacles they might be able to throw in the way, still it rose above them, and was in some measure displayed.”
We have experience of the same thing daily with respect to God; for, though he justly and reluctantly restrains his power, because the entrance to us is shut against him, yet we see that he opens up a path for himself where none exists, and ceases not to bestow favors upon us. What an amazing contest, that while we are endeavoring by every possible method to hinder the grace of God from coming to us, it rises victorious, and displays its efficacy in spite of all our exertions!

1. At that time, Herod the tetrarch heard of the fame of Jesus, 2. And said to his servants, This is John the Baptist: he is raised from the dead, and therefore miracles work in him.
 
14. And king Herod heard of him, (for his name had become celebrated,) and said, John, who baptized, hath risen from the dead, and therefore miracles are performed by him. 15. Others said, It is Elijah; and others said, It is a prophet, or as one of the prophets. 16. But when Herod heard that, he said, It is John whom I beheaded, he hath rasen from the dead.
 
7. Now Herod the tetrarch heard of all that was done by him, and was perplexed, because it was said by some that Christ had risen from the dead; 8. And by some, that Elijah had appeared; and by others, that one of the ancient prophets had risen again. 9. And Herod said, John have I beheaded, but who is this of whom I hear such things? And he desired to see him.

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="13" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. XIII.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 THe same day went Jesus out of the house, and sate by the sea-side.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 And great multitudes were gathered toge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther unto him, so that he <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luk. 5.3.</ns0:note> went into a ship, and sate, and the whole multitude stood on the shore.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark Ch.</ns0:hi> 4.1. saith, <ns0:hi>He began again to teach by the Sea-side, and there was gathered unto him a great multi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tude; so that he entred into a Ship, and sate in the Sea, and the whole multitude was by the Sea upon the Land. Luk. ch.</ns0:hi> 8.4. saith no more then, <ns0:hi>when much People were gathered together, and came to him out of every City, he speak by a Parable.</ns0:hi> Two <ns0:hi>Evangelists</ns0:hi> agree, that this Ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon of our Saviours, was Preached out of a Ship, to mul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />titudes that stood on the shore: The occasion of his going in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to a Ship, was the Throng of People, both for his own and their Convenience. It is here said, <ns0:hi>That he sate</ns0:hi>; This we observed before, was the usual Gesture of the Teacher a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mongst the <ns0:hi>Iews.</ns0:hi> This Sermon is said to have been made <ns0:hi>the same Day,</ns0:hi> which some observe in Historical Narrations, is to be taken strictly, and lets us know the Assiduity of Christ in his Work. And he spake many things to them in <ns0:hi>Parables</ns0:hi>: The term <ns0:hi>Parable</ns0:hi> often in Scripture signifies <ns0:hi>Dark</ns0:hi> sayings, or <ns0:hi>Proverbial Speeches, Ezech.</ns0:hi> 17.2. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 20.4<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. But in the Gospels it generally hath another Sense, and signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fies <ns0:hi>Similitudes</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Comparisons</ns0:hi> of things. This being the first time we have met with the term, and the first formed and perfect <ns0:hi>Parable</ns0:hi> we have met with, because we shall meet with the term often hereafter, with many formed Parables. I shall here give some notes which may be not only of use to understand the following Parables we shall meet with in this Chapter, but in the following part of the Gospel. 1. A <ns0:hi>Pa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rable</ns0:hi> (in the Gospel Sense of the term, signifieth a <ns0:hi>Simili<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tude, taken from the ordinary Actions of Men, and made use of, to inform us in one or more Points of spiritual Doctrines.</ns0:hi> 2. That it is not necessary to a Parable, <ns0:hi>That the matter con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tained in it, should be true in matter of Fact.</ns0:hi> For it is not brought to inform us in a matter of Fact; but in some spiritual truth, to which it bears some Proportion. This we see in <ns0:hi>Iotham's</ns0:hi> Parable of the <ns0:hi>Trees,</ns0:hi> going to chuse them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves a King, &c. 3. That it is not necessary, <ns0:hi>That all the Actions of Men mentioned in a Parable, should he Morally just and honest.</ns0:hi> The Actions of the unjust Steward, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 16.1, 2, 3. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> were not so. 4. That for the right under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standing of a Parable: <ns0:hi>Our great Care must be, to consi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the main Scope of it,</ns0:hi> whether the Story tends, and what our Saviour designed principally by the Parable, to instruct and teach the People by that Discourse. 5. That the main Scope of the Parable, is to be learned, either from our Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viours <ns0:hi>General,</ns0:hi> or more <ns0:hi>particular Explication of it,</ns0:hi> either, from the <ns0:hi>Proparabola,</ns0:hi> or Preface to it, or from the <ns0:hi>Epipara<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bola,</ns0:hi> or the Conclusion of it. 6. <ns0:hi>It is not to be expected, that all particular Actions represented in a Parable, should be answered by some thing in the Explication of it.</ns0:hi> 7. Last<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, though the Scope of the Parable, be the main thing we are to attend unto, and in which it doth instruct us, yet <ns0:hi>it may Collaterally inform us in several things, besides that Point which is in it, chiefly attended.</ns0:hi> It is said, that our Saviour <ns0:hi>spake many things to the Multitude in Para<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bles,</ns0:hi> covering Truths, under Similitudes, fetcht from such ordinary Actions as Men did, or might do. This was a very Ancient way of Instruction by <ns0:hi>Fables</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Parables,</ns0:hi> as we may learn by <ns0:hi>Iotham's</ns0:hi> Parable, <ns0:hi>Iud.</ns0:hi> 9.7, 8. &c. It is now much out of use with us, but amongst the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> very ordinary. So as our Saviour spake to them in their own <ns0:hi>Dialect.</ns0:hi> It had a double advantage upon the Hearers: First upon their Me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mory, we being very apt to remember Stories. 2. <ns0:hi>Vpon their Minds,</ns0:hi> to put them upon studying the meaning of what they heard, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>o delivered, and also upon their <ns0:hi>Affecti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons,</ns0:hi> Similitudes contributing much to excite Affection. But withal it had this disadvantage, that he who so taught, was not understood of a great part of his Auditory.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 And he spake many things unto them in Parables, saying, Behold<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> sower went forth to sow.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 And when he sowed, some <ns0:hi>seeds</ns0:hi> fell by the way side, and the fowls came, and devoured them up.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 Some fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth, and forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 And when the sun was up they were scorched, and because they had no root, they withered away.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 And some fell amongst thorns, and the thorns sprung up, and choked them.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 But other fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit, some an hundred fold, some sixty fold, some thirty fold.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>p. 11.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> Who hath ears to hear, let him hear.<ns0:note place="bottom">There is some difference in the terms, used by <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> in their Relations of this Parable, <ns0:hi>Mar.</ns0:hi> 4.1, 2, 3, 4, 5, <ns0:hi>& Luk.</ns0:hi> 8.4, 5, 6. But none that are material, nor much to be considered by us, being they are in the <ns0:hi>Parable.</ns0:hi> I shall when I come to it more exactly consider what differences there are betwixt the Evangelists in the terms, they use in the Explication, which our Saviour giveth us of the Parable; which he did not give before the multitude, but when he was alone (saith <ns0:hi>Mark, ch.</ns0:hi> 4.10.) That which our Saviour spoke to the whole multitude was this. Now whether there were indeed any such <ns0:hi>Sower</ns0:hi>; yea or no, is not at all ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terial: Our Saviours design was not to inform them in a mat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter of Fact, but of the different Success of the Preaching of the Word, and for this purpose he brought this Similitude, leaving the Generality of the Hearers, to study out his mean<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, concluding, <ns0:hi>He that hath Ears to hear, let him hear</ns0:hi>; which is an <ns0:hi>Epiphonema,</ns0:hi> or Conclusion of a Speech we met with before, and spake something to.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 And the disciples came, and said unto him, Why speakest thou unto them in parables?<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 8, 9. <ns0:hi>His Disciples asked him,</ns0:hi> saying, <ns0:hi>What might this Parable be? Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>When he was alone, those that were about him with the twelve, asked of him the Parable.</ns0:hi> It should seem, that his twelve Apostles un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstood his meaning, but others that with them were about him, when the multitude were gone did not: They there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore desire of him, 1. That they might understand the rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son, why he spake to the multitude in dark Sayings, and Similitudes, without plainly opening his meaning to them. 2. They own their own dulness of understanding, and con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fess that they themselves were ignorant, and therefore desired him, that he would tell them the meaning of this <ns0:hi>Parable,</ns0:hi> with which he had entertained the multitude. The<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> staying with the twelve, when the Generality of the multitudes were departed, argued that they came with a desire to lea<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, and to be in<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ructed, not out of a meer Curiosity to see Christ<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> or in a meer Formality. They shew both their Charity, in desiring others might be intelligibly instructed: And their Piety in desiring, that they might be more fully themselves instructed.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:241" />11 He answered and said unto them, Because <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 16, 17. 1 Cor. 2.10. 1 Joh. 2.27.</ns0:note> it is given to you, to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it is not given.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mar. 4.25. Luk. 19.26.</ns0:note> For whosoever hath, to him shall be gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven, and he shall have more abundance: but who<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />soever hath not: from him shall be taken, even that he hath.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 4.11. <ns0:hi>Vnto you it is given to know the Mysteries of the Kingdom of God: But unto them that are without, all these things are done in Parables, Luke</ns0:hi> saith no more then. <ns0:hi>Vnto you it is given, to know the My<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />steries of the Kingdom of God: But to them in Parables.</ns0:hi> Only <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 8.18. he saith: <ns0:hi>Take heed therefore, how you hear; for whosoever hath to him shall be given, and whoso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ever hath not, from him shall be taken, that which he seemeth to have, Because it is given to you,</ns0:hi> &c. Given by my Father, God according to the good Pleasure of his Will, hath given to some Persons to know the Mysteries of the Kingdom of God, more than to others. Some here di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stinguish concerning the things which concern the King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom of God. The Laws of his Kingdom, they say, are de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />livered plainly, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> Those things which are necessary to be known in order to our Salvation, are delivered plainly; so as we may understand them. But there are other things that belong to his Kingdom, not so necessary to be known in or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der to Salvation, these God giveth to some only to know. I cannot agree to this Notion. <ns0:hi>God manifested in the Flesh,</ns0:hi> is the <ns0:hi>Great Mystery of the Gospel,</ns0:hi> the Mystery hid from Ages, yet I am sure the knowledge of Christ, as such is ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessary to Salvation. I therefore think the Emphasis lyeth upon <ns0:hi>know.</ns0:hi> There is a more <ns0:hi>General</ns0:hi> and confused knowledge of a thing: And there is a more distinct, clear, particular, know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge. 2. There is a meer Notional knowledge, and there is a more affective, Experimental knowledge. To you my Father hath given Eternal Life, and as means in order to it, to know more clearly, particularly and distinctly, the things that concern the Kingdom of God, to know, and to believe in me, who am the Saviour of the World, my Father hath no such special and particular kindness, for the Generality of this People, and therefore he hath not given to them the same Aids and Assistances. <ns0:hi>For whosoever hath, to him it shall be given, and he shall have in more abundance: By him that hath,</ns0:hi> some understand, <ns0:hi>he that hath, and mak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth use of what he hath,</ns0:hi> and that is plainly the Sense of it. <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 25.29. where it is the <ns0:hi>Epiparobola,</ns0:hi> or Conclusion of the <ns0:hi>Parable</ns0:hi> about the <ns0:hi>Talents.</ns0:hi> But tho the preceding <ns0:hi>Pa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rable,</ns0:hi> plainly leadeth to such a Sense there, yet the preceed<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing words seem as directly to lead to another Sense here, and what is the more Natural, and proper Signification of the Word <ns0:hi>hath,</ns0:hi> which most naturally signifies to have a thing in our Possession. He that hath therefore in all reason signifies, He that <ns0:hi>hath</ns0:hi> that which <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 11. is said to be given. <ns0:hi>He that hath</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>saving knowledge</ns0:hi> of the Mysteries of the Kingdom of God. To him that doth not so much come to hear me out of Curiosity, and comprehendeth by his understanding, something of my Will, but hath an Heart that imbraceth and receiveth me, so as he believeth in me. To him that hath the <ns0:hi>Seed of God</ns0:hi> in him as in <ns0:hi>good Ground. Shall be given,</ns0:hi> that is ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pounded by the next words, <ns0:hi>and shall have in more abundance,</ns0:hi> he shall have more <ns0:hi>Grace,</ns0:hi> a more full, and clear, and distinct knowledge of me, and the things which concern my King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom. <ns0:hi>But from him that hath not,</ns0:hi> that hath not <ns0:hi>the Seed of God,</ns0:hi> a true Root of Grace, in whom the Seed of my word hath not fallen as in good Ground, but only as in the <ns0:hi>High<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />way,</ns0:hi> or in <ns0:hi>Thorny,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Stony Ground, shall be taken away, even that which he hath,</ns0:hi> how can that be? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> It must not be understood of things in the same Nature and Kind<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> expounds it <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 8.18. by <ns0:gap reason="foreign">

                     </ns0:gap>, that w<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ich either to himself, or to others he seemeth to have. He that hath not a truth of Grace, may think he hath: <ns0:hi>His hope, and Opinon of himself shall fail.</ns0:hi> Others may from his Gifts, and Parts, think <ns0:hi>he hath.</ns0:hi> God shall unmask him, taking away his common Gifts, or suffering him to fall into, and be overcome by foul Temptations. His Gifts, and Parts shall decay, his Moral righteousness will abate by Gods just Dere<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liction of him, and with-holding his restraining Grace.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 Therefore speak I to them in parables, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause they seeing, see not, and hearing hear not, neither do they understand.<ns0:note place="bottom">Neither <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> nor <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> hath this, but it directly follow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth from what they have, which also followeth here, only here it is plainly asserted concerning these Hearers, and gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven as a reason, why our Lord spake to them in Parables. We shall in the Explication of the following Words, inquire in what Sense it is said: This people <ns0:hi>seeing, saw</ns0:hi> not, and <ns0:hi>hearing, heard not.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 And in them is fulfilled the prophecy of Esaias, which saith, By hearing ye shall hear, and shall not understand; and seeing, ye shall see, and shall not perceive.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 For this peoples heart is waxen gross, and their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes they have closed, lest at any time, they should see with <ns0:hi>their</ns0:hi> eyes, and hear with <ns0:hi>their</ns0:hi> ears, and should understand with <ns0:hi>their</ns0:hi> heart, and should be con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verted, And <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap> should heal them.<ns0:note place="bottom">These words of the Prophet are not less than five times found in the new Testament (besides, by <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> in these Verses) applyed to the <ns0:hi>Iews:</ns0:hi> They are taken out of <ns0:hi>Isaiah, Ch.</ns0:hi> 6.9, 10. where they are found thus. <ns0:hi>And he said, Go, and tell this People, Hear you indeed, but understand not, and see you, but perceive not: Make the Heart of this Peop<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e fat, and their Ears heavy, and shut their Eyes, lest they see with their Eyes, and hear with their Ears, and un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstand with their Hearts, and Convert, and be healed<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     </ns0:hi> It is quoted, <ns0:hi>Mar.</ns0:hi> 4.12. <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 8.10. where the Sense of the Words only is quoted more shortly, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 12.40. <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 28.26. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 11.8. more largely, yet with some more difference of Phrase, from that of the <ns0:hi>Prophet.</ns0:hi> By all of them it ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />peareth, either, that God spake those Words to the Prophet, as well with reference to those <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> that were to live in the time of Christ: As to those <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> who were living, when <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> prophecied: Or at least, that the Words were as true of these <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> as they were of those, so the <ns0:hi>Prophecy of Isaiah</ns0:hi> was fulfilled in them.                      </ns0:gap>l, which hath several Powers and Faculties. Every thing we hear, goeth into our <ns0:hi>Heart,</ns0:hi> in some Sense. As the Heart may signify <ns0:hi>T<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> adds, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 4.19. <ns0:hi>And the Lusts of other things en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tering in, choak the Word. Luke</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 8.14. <ns0:hi>And that which fell among Thorns, are they, which when they have heard go forth, and are choked with Cares, and Riches, and Plea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sures of this Life, and bring no Fruit to perfection.</ns0:hi> Un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der these Terms, <ns0:hi>The Cares of the World, the Deceitfulness of Riches,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Pleasures of this Life,</ns0:hi> or the Lusts of other things, our Saviour comprehendeth all that which St. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> calls <ns0:hi>The Lust of the Eye,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Lust of the Flesh,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Pride of Life.</ns0:hi> The immoderate desires of our Hearts after lawful things, or their <ns0:hi>desires</ns0:hi> after things prohibited, and unlawful; these he compareth to Thorns, as Thorns in a Ground Choak <ns0:hi>the Seed,</ns0:hi> shadowing the Blade when it comes up, and keeping off the warmth of the Sun, and drawing the fatness of the Ground from it; so these divert Mens thoughts, and draw Mens Affections off from the Word of God, so as it bringeth forth no Fruit, or if there be some little appea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rance of Fruit, it dwindles away, and cometh to no perfecti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on. None of these were profane Godless Persons, who make no Conscience of negl<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>cting to hear the Word Preached. They are all Hearers. O how strait is the way? how narrow is the Gate that leadeth to Everlasting Life? how few there be that find it?</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 But he that receiveth seed into the good ground, is he that heareth the word, and under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standeth <ns0:hi>it,</ns0:hi> which also beareth fruit, and bringeth forth some an hundred fold, some sixty, some thirty.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 4.20. much the same. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     </ns0:hi> 8.15. <ns0:hi>But that on the good Ground, are they, which in an honest and good Heart, having heard the Word keep it,</ns0:hi> and bring forth Fruit <ns0:hi>with patience.</ns0:hi> To make a good Christian, all these things must Concur. 1. An <ns0:hi>hearing of the Word.</ns0:hi> 2. An <ns0:hi>understanding</ns0:hi> or believing it. 3. A <ns0:hi>keeping of it.</ns0:hi> 4. A <ns0:hi>bringing forth of Fruit.</ns0:hi> 5 A <ns0:hi>bringing forth Fruit with patience.</ns0:hi> He that receiveth the Seed into good Ground, is he (saith <ns0:hi>Luke) who in an honest and good Heart, having heard the Word keep it.</ns0:hi> The good ground in this Parable, is the <ns0:hi>go<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>d</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>honest heart,</ns0:hi> that is, an Heart renewed, and sanctified <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
